# zero core: design of the Rust core for zero-server

Date: 2026-09-30. Status: final design synthesized from the three architecture proposals (arch-performance-first.md, arch-pragmatic-fast.md, arch-binding-first.md) and the three judge verdicts, all in this directory, then revised in place against three adversarial reviews (performance against the official Round 23 run, security and dependency policy, feasibility and effort); section 20 lists every review issue and the change made.

How the synthesis was made. The judges scored the proposals on three lenses: raw performance and hardware efficiency (winner arch-performance-first, 8 against 6.5 and 7.5), security and dependency risk (winner arch-pragmatic-fast, 8 against 5 and 6.5), and binding ergonomics and time to a credible first release (winner arch-pragmatic-fast, 8 against 4 and 7). The aggregate is arch-pragmatic-fast 22.5, arch-binding-first 21.0, arch-performance-first 17.0, and two of the three judges chose arch-pragmatic-fast, so its skeleton is the base: a fixed owned-buffer runtime seam, a crate-backed driver in the first release, in-house no_std codecs above it, rustls for TLS, quinn-proto behind a feature for QUIC. Onto that base this document grafts every item the judges recommended: the binding-first FFI boundary (53-bit slot ids, total accessors, one batch descriptor, one wake per batch), the binding-first zero-rt, zero-limits, zero-policy and zero-template crates, the performance-first measurement gates, counting-allocator test, io_uring operator posture and zero-sys isolation rule, the compio-driver adapter as the permanent driver baseline in the unpublished bench crate, the system allocator in every binding, honesty on updates q=1, the issue 8790 resilience gate, the generated C header plus .NET and Python smoke tests in the first release, and the corrections the judges asked for (the Windows mio statement, the exact tokio feature set, the unverified status of the Google kCTF figures). Where two judges disagreed (whether compio-driver ships as the first driver or waits in the bench crate), section 5 records the resolution and the reason.

Evidence rule. Every technical statement below is backed by one of three things: a source fetched in this task (listed in section 19 with what it said), a measurement run in this task (the three binding probes rerun on 2026-09-30 and the Round 23 extraction rerun over the local round23-ph.json, outputs saved as rerun-*.txt beside this file), or an explicit "carried from" reference to one of the research files in this directory, which record their own sources but were not re-fetched here. Anything else is marked unverified. Effort figures and expected throughput bands are judgment and are labeled as such. Round 23 numbers are the "Continuous Benchmarking Run 2025-01-30 18:47:41" values in round23-ph.json as extracted by tfb-extract2.js in this task.

## 1. Purpose and goals in priority order

The product is a new native core for zero-server, written in Rust, exposed to TypeScript (Node), Python and C# through idiomatic bindings, and shaped like the owner's pamoja repository at C:\Users\tonyw\Desktop\projects\zero-edge. The existing Node implementation (@zero-server/sdk 1.1.0) keeps its users, its standards registry and its test corpus; the core replaces its implementation underneath the same package name over two releases (section 15).

Goals, in the owner's priority order, and the single sentence each one resolves to in this design:

1. Faster than Drogon on TechEmpower-style workloads. Precisely: the Rust tier 4 entry beats Drogon; declarative tier 0 to 2 routes in every language inherit that number because no host code runs on their request path; host-language (tier 3) handlers are scored against the best entry of that language in Round 23 (uwebsockets.js for Node, aspnetcore for C#, the best Python entry), never against Drogon, because the json test forbids cached serialization and requires the object to be instantiated per request (wiki, fetched), so a Node, Python or C# json handler is tier 3 by rule. Two exceptions hold on the Rust entry itself: updates q=1, where the deliverable is parity (every Realistic Rust entry lands at 1.04 to 1.05 times Drogon), and plaintext, where the best-level deliverable is the link ceiling with zero errors and the 256-connection deliverable is parity plus zero errors (no Realistic tokio entry exceeds 1.06 times Drogon at that level; section 13). Reached by adopting the technique matrix of the Round 23 leaders (in-house zero-copy HTTP/1.1 parser with SIMD scans, prebuilt status and header blocks, per-core cached Date, allocation-free Content-Length, one writev per pipelined burst, buffer-direct JSON and template writers, one PostgreSQL connection per core with every statement written before the first read, pre-generated single-statement updates, worker per logical CPU with affinity), not by the choice of kernel I/O backend: the same ntex code on tokio and on compio landed within 5 to 10 percent either way in Round 23 (section 13).
2. Fully non-blocking I/O. Every socket operation runs on the per-core event loop; the only blocking work (SQLite, file reads that cannot use a kernel file-send path) runs on dedicated threads behind bounded channels and never on a request path.
3. Low hardware usage, CPU and memory per connection. Thread-per-core with no work stealing and no Send bound, a per-core arena that keeps tiers 0 to 2 and 4 free of global-allocator calls (asserted by a counting allocator over the real request path including the handler ABI), a receive buffer leased from the per-core pool only between readiness and the read and returned while the connection is idle with no partial head (so an idle connection holds no receive buffer on the readiness backends too, section 5.6), and measurement gates (bytes per idle connection at 10k, 100k and 1M connections; cgroup CPU per request) recorded on the first driver and used to judge every later driver, because no fetched source publishes either figure for any Rust runtime.
4. Maximum security. Reject-not-normalize framing on both directions (inbound parser and outbound serializer), a limit table with configurable defaults, `unsafe_code = "forbid"` outside the audited crates of section 10.1 (six workspace crates plus the two Rust binding crates), a cross-thread slot ownership contract enforced by an atomic state word (section 7.3), per-parser fuzz targets, a populated cargo-deny allowlist that denies every unlisted crate, cargo-vet, cargo-auditable, SLSA Build L3 provenance, `panic = "unwind"` with `catch_unwind` at every FFI export, the system allocator inside every host process, and the io_uring path off by default in the shipped graph until it is measured and documented for operators.
5. no_std wherever the code needs no operating system. Every codec, parser, router, limit table, date formatter and writer is `#![no_std]` plus `alloc`, proven by a host build with `--no-default-features` and a bare-metal cross-compile in CI; the I/O layer, TLS I/O, drivers, FFI and bindings are std by decision.
6. One Rust core with idiomatic TypeScript, Python and C# bindings, exactly in the pamoja shape: `crates/`, `bindings/node`, `bindings/python`, `bindings/dotnet`, an ffi crate with a generated C header, `conformance/vectors.json`, `cargo xtask`, Docker-run rustfmt and clippy, cargo-deny, release workflows for crates.io, npm, PyPI and NuGet.

## 2. The premise: Node is already non-blocking, so where is the gap

Node's I/O is not the problem. libuv's design page (fetched) states that "All (network) I/O is performed on non-blocking sockets which are polled using the best mechanism available on the given platform: epoll on Linux, kqueue on OSX and other BSDs, event ports on SunOS and IOCP on Windows", that "Network I/O is always performed in a single thread, each loop's thread", and that blocking file I/O runs in a thread pool. That is the same readiness model tokio uses through mio, and Drogon's Trantor uses epoll and kqueue (carried from salvage-map.md, Drogon README). A Rust core does not win by being non-blocking; it wins by doing less work per request and by doing that work on every core.

What the Round 23 data says (measured in this task with tfb-extract2.js over round23-ph.json; requests per second at the best concurrency level):

| Entry | plaintext | json | db | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| nodejs (bare http module) | 1,460,302 (3,488 errors) | 1,147,305 | 371,704 (nodejs-postgresjs-raw) | one JavaScript thread per process, cluster of processes |
| uwebsockets.js | 27,991,649 | 2,731,253 | 711,561 (uwebsockets.js-postgres) | C++ core under a thin JavaScript layer; the entry forks one cluster worker per CPU (`os.availableParallelism()`, frameworks/JavaScript/uwebsockets.js/src/clustered.js, fetched), so it runs 56 JavaScript threads with the handler called inline on the C++ event loop thread and no cross-thread hop; postgres.js still runs in JavaScript |
| ultimate-express | 27,324,164 | 1,568,342 | 524,416 | Express-compatible layer over uWebSockets.js |
| drogon | 14,655,006 | 2,474,350 | 1,033,970 (drogon-core) | C++ on epoll, one connection per event loop |
| ntex-plt / ntex-db (tokio, one current-thread runtime per core) | 24,925,516 | 2,963,471 | 1,294,048 | the runtime shape this design ships first |
| may-minihttp (epoll, stackful coroutines) | 27,906,423 (974 errors) | 3,102,063 | 1,357,757 | leads json, query and fortunes among Rust entries |
| faf, libreactor (bare epoll) | 28,034,705, 28,025,993 | | | the 40 GbE link ceiling, zero errors |

Three conclusions follow. First, a C++ core under Node reaches the plaintext ceiling (uwebsockets.js at 27.99M, 5 percent below faf) because plaintext is link-bound: the Round 23 announcement (fetched) reports the hardware as an Intel Xeon Gold 6330 with 56 cores, 64 GB and a Mellanox ConnectX-6 40 Gbps adapter, and "4x Improvements in Theoretical Network-Bound Tests" over the 10 GbE previous round, and eleven entries from five languages cluster between 27.53M and 28.38M in the extraction. Second, the moment JavaScript is on the per-request path the gap opens: uwebsockets.js drops to 2.73M on json (8 percent below ntex-plt, 6 percent below hyper) and to 712K on db (45 percent below ntex-db), because the JSON object and the PostgreSQL wire protocol are still executed in JavaScript, even with one JavaScript thread per core and the handler called inline with no thread hop. That entry is the Node yardstick and it is a structurally strong one: any Node model with fewer JavaScript threads than cores, or with a thread crossing per batch, starts behind it on json (section 8.5 states how the Node binding answers this). Third, bare Node at 1.46M plaintext with 3,488 errors is 5 percent of the link, so the existing zero-server, which the salvage work measured at 71 to 72 percent of bare `node:http` with its default debug logging on and a linear regex router at 10.9 microseconds per miss with 400 routes (carried from salvage-map.md section 2.7, not re-measured here), starts two orders of magnitude below the target.

The boundary cost is the other half of the premise. Measured in this task on the owner's Windows 11 desktop (Node v24.13.0 x64, CPython 3.13.1 GIL build, .NET 10.0.2). Every figure below is a Windows wall-clock number; the ThreadsafeFunction rows are dominated by libuv async wake latency, which is an operating-system property, so the Node budgets, the batch-size rule and the tier 3 bands derived from them are provisional until the same three probes are rerun in `node:24`, `python:3.13` and `mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk` Linux containers, which section 12.5 makes a precondition of freezing release 1 planning (the probes and their runners are in this directory and need no change to run under Linux):

| Crossing | Node | Python | .NET |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Synchronous call into Rust, no arguments | 12.0 ns | 22.7 ns | 4.5 ns (`[LibraryImport]`), 3.0 ns with `[SuppressGCTransition]` |
| Borrowed byte view of a 256-byte body | 58.6 ns (`Buffer` slice) | 53.0 ns (`&[u8]`) | 1.3 ns (span over Rust memory) |
| One finalizable object per request | 825.9 ns (`External`), 821.1 ns (external `Buffer`) | 196.4 ns (`#[pyclass]`) | not applicable (struct by pointer) |
| One Promise or awaitable per request, pipelined | 1,836 ns at 64 in flight (544,554 per second), 1,873 ns at 256 | | |
| Rust worker thread to host callback, one per request | 507 to 527 ns at 64 to 1,024 in flight (ThreadsafeFunction), 13,938 ns sequential | 2,219 ns per call when attaching per call | 2.7 ns reverse P/Invoke, 11,100 ns once per fresh native thread |
| Same callback, attached once, batched items per crossing, one batch in flight | 1,183 ns per item at 16, 374 ns at 64, 125 ns at 256 (7.98M items per second) | 36 ns per call attached; 20, 18 and 16 ns per item at 16, 64 and 256 | 2.7 ns per call after the one-time attach |
| Same batched callback with several batches in flight (rerun-node-probe-inflight.txt, measured in this revision) | per item at 1, 2, 4 and 8 batches in flight: 1 item 19,273, 8,043, 2,287, 1,174 ns; 4 items 4,801, 1,744, 611, 342 ns; 8 items 2,218, 593, 232, 187 ns; 16 items 1,170, 124, 120, 114 ns; 64 items 326, 123, 69, 63 ns | not rerun (the Python crossing is a same-thread call once attached, so in-flight count does not apply) | not applicable (same-thread reverse P/Invoke) |
| Decoding a 24-byte path to a host string | 87.4 ns (`reqPath` returning a String) | 47.8 ns | 18.0 ns |

So a design that hands each request to the host language as an object, awaits a Promise per request and hops a thread per request spends about 1.8 to 2.7 microseconds of pure boundary cost per request in Node, which alone caps one isolate near 530K requests per second (the measured Promise-per-request ceiling), a fraction of the 2.9M json figure of the Rust entries. The same handler reached through batched crossings, with the request identified by an integer slot id and read through pooled view objects, costs 16 ns per request in Python and single-digit nanoseconds in .NET. In Node the per-item wall cost is set by how many items are in flight at the target isolate, not by the batch size alone: 256 items per crossing measure 125 ns, but so do 16 items per crossing with two batches in flight (124 ns), while 8 items with one batch in flight cost 2,218 ns and one item with one in flight 19,273 ns (rerun-node-probe-inflight.txt). The TechEmpower json and db tests run non-pipelined at 16 to 512 connections (wiki, fetched), so at most 512 requests are in flight cluster-wide, about 9 per core on 56 workers; a Node model that queues per core and dispatches to one isolate per core therefore sees batches of 1 to 9 with one or two in flight, which is the 600 to 2,300 ns region of the table, and the 125 ns figure is reachable only when many workers feed one isolate. What the probe measures is wall time, not CPU per item; the CPU cost of a libuv wake is unmeasured and is a section 5.7 gate. Section 8.5 draws the consequence: the default Node deployment is one isolate per core fed by its own worker, the same 56-thread shape as uwebsockets.js, and the crossing latency at 9 in flight (about 2 microseconds against a 164 to 207 microsecond round trip at 512 connections) is a throughput cost only through its CPU share, which is what the harness measures. That is the gap the core closes: not the I/O model but the per-request CPU work (parsing, routing, policy, serialization, the database wire protocol) and the number and shape of the boundary crossings. Everything expressible as data (routes, static responses, cache specifications, query plans, policy rules) runs in Rust without a crossing; handlers that must be host code are reached once per batch.

## 4. Workspace and crate layout

Repository shape, copied from pamoja (section 14 lists what is verbatim): Cargo workspace with `resolver = "2"`, `crates/<name>` with one responsibility per crate, `[workspace.lints]` inherited by every member, `bindings/node`, `bindings/python`, `bindings/dotnet` excluded from the workspace with their own lockfiles, `conformance/vectors.json` generated by the examples crate and asserted by all three bindings, `docs/capabilities.toml` claiming every library crate exactly once, `docs/standards.toml` as the conformance registry, `deny.toml`, `justfile`, `rust-toolchain.toml`, `.cargo/config.toml` with the `xtask` alias, and the release workflows.

Legend: N = `#![cfg_attr(not(feature = "std"), no_std)]` plus `alloc`, built with `--no-default-features` and cross-compiled for thumbv7em-none-eabihf in CI; S = std; A = audited crate (`unsafe_code = "deny"` with per-item allows and `// SAFETY:` comments); R1, R2, R3 = the release it first ships in (section 4.4).

### 4.3 The no_std rule and its proof

A crate is no_std plus alloc when its inputs and outputs are byte slices, buffers or plain values and it never needs a clock, a socket, a file, a thread or an operating-system event queue (carried from research-nostd-and-security.md section 3). Each such crate carries `#![cfg_attr(not(feature = "std"), no_std)]`, `extern crate alloc`, `default = ["std"]`, and forbids `unsafe_code`; `zero-simd` is the one no_std crate allowed unsafe, and its unsafe inventory has two parts: the dispatch call site (Rust 1.86 stabilized `#[target_feature]` on safe functions, carried from research-http-and-ws.md) and every pointer-taking load and store inside the kernels (`_mm256_loadu_si256`, `_mm_loadu_si128`, `vld1q_u8` and their stores), because Rust 1.87 made safe only the intrinsics "that are unsafe only due to requiring target features to be enabled" (release notes, fetched), and a pointer load carries its own safety obligation. Each such block carries a `// SAFETY:` comment stating the bounds check that precedes it, and the count of those blocks is part of the cargo-geiger release inventory. `#![no_std]` alone proves nothing because a dependency may still link std, so CI proves it two ways: a host build with `--no-default-features` and a bare-metal cross-compile for thumbv7em-none-eabihf (the pamoja `embedded` job).

Primitive injection. Several no_std crates need a digest, a MAC, a KDF or random bytes (`zero-jwt` for signing and verification, `zero-totp` for HMAC, `zero-pg-proto` for SCRAM's SHA-256, HMAC, PBKDF2 and nonce, `zero-trace` for trace ids, `zero-cookie` for signed cookies, `zero-ws` for the SHA-1 accept value), and the implementations live in `zero-server-crypto`, which is std because it wraps aws-lc-rs. A no_std crate never depends on it. `zero-core` defines the `Digest`, `Mac`, `Kdf` and `Rng` traits, each no_std crate that needs a primitive takes an implementation as a generic parameter or a function table at construction, `zero-server-crypto` implements the traits on the std side, and every such crate carries a no_std test with a pure-Rust test-only implementation (a reference SHA-256 and HMAC under `cfg(test)`) so the `--no-default-features` build exercises the real code path. The crates that require injection are exactly the six named here, listed in `docs/capabilities.toml` under an `injects` key so the list is checked, not remembered. rustls itself is `#![no_std]` with `#![forbid(unsafe_code, unused_must_use)]` (its lib.rs, fetched) and exposes an unbuffered API, but its QUIC types are std-only and aws-lc-rs is std-only, so the TLS handshake runs with `std` on in production and the no_std path through the ring provider is a portability guarantee rather than the shipped build (carried from research-tls-and-deps.md sections 3 and 8.2).

### 4.4 Releases

Release 1 (the first credible release): HTTP/1.1 with pipelining, static files, router, WebSocket and SSE with their host-side ABI (receive events, send, close, backpressure), TLS through rustls on both seam drivers, tier 0 policy subset, tiers 3 and 4, the `zero-ffi` C ABI with the generated header, the slot ownership protocol, `zero-sys`, the Node binding with the per-core isolate pool and the TypeScript facade, a .NET smoke test and a Python smoke import over the same cdylib, the `zero-h3` and `zero-qpack` codecs with vectors, the two TechEmpower entries for plaintext and json, the self-run harness of section 12.5 (run for release 1 by the desktop method recorded there), the Linux rerun of the three binding probes, and the measurement gates recorded on `io-tokio` and `io-compio`. Release 1 tier 3 handlers are buffered only: a request body arrives complete (up to the route's body limit) and a response body is handed over in one call; there is no incremental read, no `res.write` followed by `res.end`, and no chunked write from a host handler. Proxy routes, uploads above the body limit and long responses from host code are therefore not release 1 features.

Release 2: HTTP/2 in house, streaming request and response bodies on the handler ABI (`zero_req_body_read` plus a body-chunk event on the batch path, `zero_res_write` and `zero_res_end` over the chunked encoder with a writable status), PostgreSQL driver and tier 2 data routes (db, query, updates, fortunes on the harness, published on both `io-tokio` and `io-compio`), `zero-template`, tier 1 cache, the remaining policy rules, JWT verification and JWKS with the trust store requirement, sessions, body parsers, kTLS, OCSP with full response verification, mTLS with CRLs, the Python facade with its handler thread pool, the C# facade with its managed thread per core, both packages, the Node inline-loop experiment of section 8.5, `zero migrate` and `zero doctor`.

Release 3: HTTP/3 and QUIC behind `http3` (compiled in, runtime-off; Windows functional only, section 6.5), MySQL and MariaDB, MongoDB, Redis, SQLite, the ORM layer, the auth stack, gRPC, observability, WebRTC signaling, compression, the plugin loader with its trust model, the Node-compatible request and response emulation for the vitest subset that needs it (section 12.3), and the parity gate against zero-server 1.1.0 (section 15).

## 5. Runtime and I/O model per operating system

### 5.1 The contract

One worker thread per logical CPU (`available_parallelism()`, overridable with a `threads` option), each owning a single-threaded executor, its own listener where the operating system allows one, its own request arena, its own database connections and its own cache shard; tasks are `!Send`; there is no work stealing; a connection lives on the core that accepted it for its whole lifetime; every buffer that crosses an await is owned, never borrowed; cross-core traffic exists only as explicit wakes for accept handoff (Windows, macOS), WebSocket room fan-out, cache tag invalidation, shutdown and migrated QUIC datagrams, never on the request path of a connection-local handler. Host handler threads (a Node isolate, the Python handler thread, a managed .NET thread) are paired one to one with workers and read worker-owned slots only through the borrow protocol of section 7.3; a worker never attaches to a host runtime and never runs host code (section 8).

This is the shape of the Round 23 Rust entries that beat Drogon on every test they entered: ntex-plt, hyper and axum build one tokio current-thread runtime per core with an SO_REUSEPORT listener each, and xitca-web-unrealistic does the same (attribution carried from research-techempower.md section 3.1, which fetched the TFB sources). tokio's runtime documentation (fetched, 1.53.1) describes the current-thread scheduler as two FIFO queues (global and local), no LIFO slot, tasks woken from inside the runtime going to the local queue, and the I/O and timer drivers polled "whenever there are no tasks ready to be scheduled, or when it has scheduled 61 tasks in a row" (`event_interval`), which is exactly the single-threaded, no-stealing behavior the bindings and the arena rely on. Rejected shapes: tokio multi-thread (work stealing, Send bound, LIFO slot; no Round 23 Rust leader runs it), glommio (Linux only), may (a stack per connection and thread-local hazards across yields), SQPOLL and IOPOLL (a kernel polling thread and busy-waiting respectively, per the io_uring_setup man page fetched; both burn idle CPU, which conflicts with goal 3).

### 5.2 The seam: `zero-io`

`zero-io` is the only crate that names a third-party runtime, and its traits are fixed from the first commit so that every later backend is a drop-in: `Runtime::spawn_local`, `Listener::accept`, `Stream::read_into(OwnedBuf) -> (Result<usize>, OwnedBuf)`, `Stream::write(OwnedBuf) -> (Result<usize>, OwnedBuf)`, `Stream::writev(&[IoSlice<'_>])` over a fixed-capacity iovec array that lives in the per-core slab (the readiness backends pass it to `try_write_vectored` directly; the completion backend copies the descriptors into its owned submission, which is the one place a completion backend pays for the seam), `Datagram::recv_batch` and `Datagram::send_batch` with per-datagram ECN, destination and segment size (present from release 1 so QUIC never forces a seam change), `Timer`, `DateService`, `Shutdown`. The readiness backends perform the read on readiness into an owned buffer leased from the per-core pool at that moment (`readable()`, lease, `try_read`) and return the buffer to the pool when the connection goes idle with no partial head, so an idle connection holds no receive buffer on epoll and kqueue either (section 5.6); this is the direction compio's polling driver already takes (carried from research-runtime-io.md section 7.1), so the contract costs nothing on epoll and kqueue and is what a completion backend requires: the io-uring crate documents that an entry's parameters "such as buffer" must be "valid for the entire duration of the operation, otherwise it may cause memory problems" (docs.rs io-uring 0.7.15, `SubmissionQueue::push`, fetched), and an owned-buffer seam is the only way to keep that guarantee out of the HTTP layer.

### 5.3 Driver sequencing, and the resolution of the judges' disagreement

The performance judge asked that compio-driver be the first shipped driver (native IOCP on Windows, io_uring with a polling fallback on Linux, no low-concurrency step in the Round 23 data). The security and binding judges asked that tokio ship first and compio stay in the unpublished bench crate until it passes the gates and moves past its beta line, because compio-driver is pre-1.0 and single-organization. All three agreed on the facts: the same ntex code on tokio and on compio landed within 5 to 10 percent either way (plaintext 24,925,516 against 23,164,471, json 2,963,471 against 2,899,760, db 1,294,048 against 1,334,739, query 1,378,950 against 1,245,795, fortunes 1,134,702 against 1,197,352, updates 474,071 against 477,805, all from the extraction rerun in this task), so the driver does not set the TechEmpower number; and no fetched source quantifies CPU per request or bytes per connection for either.

Resolution:

- Release 1 ships `io-tokio` as the default backend of every published artifact. Exact feature set: `tokio = { version = "1", default-features = false, features = ["rt", "net", "time", "sync", "io-util"] }`, no `macros`, no `rt-multi-thread`, no `fs` (file reads go through the blocking-thread path or the backend's file-send primitive); the graph measured in this task's predecessor (measure-tokio-tree.txt, cargo 1.96.0, 2026-09-30) is 6 crates on Linux and macOS (tokio 1.53.1, mio 1.2.3, socket2 0.6.5, libc 0.2.189, bytes 1.12.1, pin-project-lite 0.2.17) and 7 on Windows (windows-sys 0.61.2 and windows-link 0.2.1 replacing libc). Whether the `io-util` feature adds a crate to that measured `rt` set is unverified until the allowlist is frozen with a `cargo tree` on the real manifest.
- `io-compio` is built in the workspace from release 1 as a non-default cargo feature of `zero-io`, runs the full test matrix with the same weight as `io-tokio`, and is the permanent comparison baseline in `zero-bench`, so the self-run against Drogon happens before any custom reactor exists and every later driver change is measured against a crate-backed driver. Facts fetched on compio-driver: max stable version 0.12.5 with 0.13.0-beta.1 published 2026-09-29 (crates.io), MIT, 1,008,620 downloads; its `Proactor` "owns the operations to keep the driver safe"; it provides `BufferPool` and `BufferAllocator`; feature flags `io-uring` (default, io-uring ^0.7.13), `polling` (^3.3.0), `iocp-global`, `iocp-wait-packet`, `io-uring-sqe128`, `io-uring-cqe32`; its `op` module exposes `AcceptMulti`, `RecvMulti`, `RecvMsgMulti`, `RecvManaged`, `RecvMsgManaged`, `SendMsgZc`, `SendVectoredZc` and `Splice`. Whether `RecvManaged` uses an io_uring provided buffer ring (IORING_REGISTER_PBUF_RING) is unverified; it is checked in the source before the idle-memory gate is interpreted.
- `io-compio` becomes the default on a platform only when all of the following hold: the section 5.7 gates show a CPU-per-request or bytes-per-idle-connection advantage on that platform against `io-tokio` with lazy buffer leasing (not against a naive one-buffer-per-connection policy); the 16-connection difference is reproduced and its cause identified; compio-driver is on a stable line covered by cargo-vet; and, on Windows, the mio path has been measured (section 5.4). Until then the shipped graph carries no io-uring, polling or compio crate, which is what the security judge asked for.
- A custom in-house reactor (the performance-first proposal's `zero-reactor` and `zero-sys`) is deferred to after release 3 and enters only behind the same seam, under the conditions in section 5.5.

### 5.4 Per operating system

Linux. One `SO_REUSEPORT` listener per core created with socket2 (`set_reuse_port(true)`, as hyper's and axum's TFB entries do; carried), backlog 1024 (ntex and actix; carried), `TCP_NODELAY` on accepted sockets, `TCP_DEFER_ACCEPT` and `TCP_FASTOPEN` as listener options, thread affinity through `sched_setaffinity`, optional `SO_INCOMING_CPU` behind a setting (carried from research-runtime-io.md section 2b); every one of these that socket2 does not expose as a safe method is a safe wrapper in `zero-sys`, never a `libc` call inside `zero-io`. `io-tokio` is epoll through mio. `io-compio` is io_uring through compio's fusion driver with the polling (epoll) fallback taken when `io_uring_setup` returns EPERM or ENOSYS. Docker's default seccomp profile blocks `io_uring_setup`, `io_uring_enter` and `io_uring_register`, each "due to security vulnerabilities that can be exploited to break out of containers" (docs.docker.com, fetched), removed by moby/moby PR 46762 merged 2023-11-02 and released in Docker 25.0.0 (fetched; the PR text also states that Google disabled io_uring on ChromeOS, Android and its production servers). The epoll path is therefore the path most container deployments take, and it is tested with the same weight as any completion backend; the operator documentation carries an io_uring note and the `--io=epoll` switch (section 10.6). Nothing in the benchmark depends on io_uring: faf and libreactor reach the 28.0M plaintext ceiling on bare epoll (extraction).

Windows. Windows has no `SO_REUSEPORT` listener group and Microsoft documents `SO_REUSEADDR` as unsafe for servers (carried from research-runtime-io.md, learn.microsoft.com), so one listener with `SO_EXCLUSIVEADDRUSE` accepts on core 0 and hands each accepted socket round-robin to a per-core runtime (`TcpStream::from_std` on `io-tokio`); affinity through `SetThreadAffinityMask` in `zero-sys` (windows-sys is already in the tokio Windows graph, measured). `io-compio` brings one IOCP per core with `GetQueuedCompletionStatusEx` batches and a pre-posted `AcceptEx` pool (carried from research-runtime-io.md 1.4 and 2b) and `TransmitFile` for static files. The cost of the mio path on Windows is recorded as unverified rather than asserted: the docs.rs mio 1.2.3 `Poll` implementation notes say that on Windows "calls to `read` and `write` require data to be copied into an intermediate buffer before it is passed to the kernel", while the mio README says "The Windows implementation for polling sockets is using the wepoll strategy. This uses the Windows AFD system to access socket readiness events" (both fetched); the two statements from the same project describe different mechanisms, so the actual per-read cost is measured on the harness with `io-tokio` against `io-compio` before any Windows number is published. This replaces risk 6 of the pragmatic proposal, as the security judge asked. Windows is a development and deployment platform; the benchmark platform is Linux.

macOS. kqueue through mio (`io-tokio`) or polling (`io-compio`); Apple's `SO_REUSEPORT` does not distribute TCP connections (carried), so the Windows accept-handoff shape is reused; `sendfile(2)` with headers and trailers arrives with `io-compio`; no thread pinning, because a supported macOS affinity API is unverified. FreeBSD is not a tier-one target; if built there, `SO_REUSEPORT_LB` per-core listeners apply (carried).

### 5.5 The custom io_uring backend, kept as a specification

The performance-first proposal's Linux backend is retained as the specification for a later `io-uring` backend behind the seam: ring flags `IORING_SETUP_SINGLE_ISSUER` (6.0, "a hint to the kernel that only a single task (or thread) will submit requests"), `IORING_SETUP_DEFER_TASKRUN` (6.1, defers work until an `io_uring_enter` with `IORING_ENTER_GETEVENTS`) and `IORING_SETUP_COOP_TASKRUN` (5.19, reduces interruptions of a task running in userspace) (io_uring_setup man page, fetched); the ring fd registered (`IORING_REGISTER_RING_FDS`, 5.18, at most 16 registered ring descriptors) and hot files registered (`IORING_REGISTER_FILES`, 5.1); one provided buffer ring per core (`IORING_REGISTER_PBUF_RING`, 5.19, with the `IOU_PBUF_RING_INC` incremental-consumption flag) (io_uring_register man page, fetched); multishot accept, multishot recv over the buffer ring, `msg_ring` wakes, `link_timeout` deadlines and `IORING_ASYNC_CANCEL_ALL` on shutdown (carried from research-runtime-io.md sections 1.1 and 2b); flag downgrades on 5.19 and 6.0 and the epoll fallback below 5.19 or on EPERM and ENOSYS. Under that backend an idle connection holds no receive buffer at all, because the kernel picks a buffer from the ring only when data arrives. The shipped readiness backend reaches the same idle state by leasing the buffer on readiness and returning it when the connection is idle (section 5.6), so the provided buffer ring is not the mechanism behind the memory-per-connection goal; what it can still buy is fewer syscalls and wakeups per byte, which is a CPU question, not a memory one. Rules if it is built: every raw operating-system declaration (io_uring uapi structs, Winsock extension pointers) joins `zero-sys`, which exists from release 1 as the audited leaf crate for every raw call (section 4.2); the reactor crate gets Miri with strict provenance and many seeds where it can run without syscalls, ASan and TSan jobs, and a structure-aware fuzz target over operation sequences; the tokio-rs io-uring crate stays a dev-dependency used as a differential oracle on SQE bytes. Entry criteria: the section 5.7 gates show a CPU-per-request or bytes-per-idle-connection advantage of compio's io_uring path over `io-tokio` running the lazy-lease policy at 10k, 100k and 1M connections (the naive one-buffer-per-connection number is not the comparison) that an in-house backend can plausibly widen (the only published runtime comparison that states CPU is monoio's echo benchmark, fetched: Xeon Gold 5118, 10 GbE, peak throughput "about twice" tokio at 4 cores and "close to 3 times" at 16, "the lowest latency and CPU usage" as connections increase, higher latency than tokio with few connections on one core; it is not HTTP), and an owner decision that accepts the unsafe budget of section 10.1.

### 5.6 Buffers, timers, executor, shutdown, allocator

- Buffers: receive buffers are 8 KiB blocks in a per-core pool, leased to a connection when it becomes readable and returned when the connection is idle with no partial head and no unread body, grown on demand to the head cap while a head is being read; an idle connection therefore holds its connection record, its slot in the pipelining ring and its timer entry, and no receive buffer, on every backend. The bytes-per-idle-connection gate of section 5.7 is recorded with this policy on `io-tokio` at 10k, 100k and 1M connections in release 1, and that number, not the naive 8 KiB per connection (8 GiB at the 1M gate), is what a completion backend must beat. Write buffers are per-core slabs with the fixed-capacity iovec array of section 5.2; a response is serialized into the connection's write buffer and large bodies are passed as separate iovecs rather than copied; connection state, request slots, header tables and write buffers live in per-core arenas that are chunked and never reallocated (section 7.3) so tiers 0 to 2 and 4 make zero calls to the global allocator per request, asserted by a counting allocator that drives the real request path including the handler ABI (accept, parse, route, handler, serialize, writev) from release 1 (the performance-first graft every judge asked to keep). A per-core request-memory budget in `zero-limits` (section 10.4) pauses accepts on that core when leased receive buffers plus buffered bodies exceed it, so the body limit times the connection count is not the committed-memory bound.
- Timers: tokio's hierarchical wheel (carried: six levels of 64 slots, 1 ms precision, which meets RFC 9002's `kGranularity` for QUIC pacing). One `DateService` per core refreshes a 37-byte `Date: ...\r\n` block every second; the TechEmpower requirements state that "All test types require `Server` and `Date` HTTP response headers" (wiki, fetched) and the verifier tolerance recorded in research-techempower.md is 3 seconds (carried).
- Executor: tokio current-thread with a `LocalSet`; one spawned task per connection, and tier 4 handler futures are polled inline inside that connection task (the ntex dispatcher shape), never spawned per request, because tokio documents that every spawned task "require[s] only a single allocation and 64 bytes of memory" (tokio.rs tutorial, fetched) and one allocation per request is exactly what the counting-allocator assertion forbids; `spawn_local` is used only for detached work (a handler that explicitly forks a background job, room fan-out, driver tasks). Request state is `Rc`; the Date block, the per-core database connection and the tier 1 shard are thread-local values reached without atomics. The one atomic on the request path is the per-slot ownership state word of section 7.3, which exists because host threads read slots the worker owns.
- Shutdown: stop accepting, set the per-core cancellation flag, drain in-flight requests to a deadline, then either wait unbounded or `shutdown_timeout` (carried from research-runtime-io.md section 5.3). The core never installs signal handlers inside a host process; the bindings wire Node process signals, the Python `signal` module and .NET `PosixSignalRegistration` to the single shutdown entry point (section 8.4).
- Allocator: the system allocator in every cdylib; the core never sets a global allocator inside a binding. `zero-serve` and `zero-bench` offer an `alloc-mimalloc` feature (every Round 23 leader ships mimalloc or snmalloc, carried from research-techempower.md section 7.3), which adds the C graph measured in measure-tokio-tree.txt (mimalloc 0.1.52, libmimalloc-sys 0.1.49, cc 1.5.1, shlex 2.0.1, find-msvc-tools 0.1.14). Its effect inside Node, Python and .NET hosts is measured on the harness (section 12.5) before the bindings offer it even as an opt-in; the per-core arenas are what keep the choice off the hot path.

### 5.7 Measurement gates recorded on the first driver

Recorded in release 1 on `io-tokio` and `io-compio` on the same binary and hardware, and re-recorded for every later driver: bytes per idle connection at 10k, 100k and 1M connections per backend with the lazy-lease policy (no published figure exists for any Rust runtime); CPU per request with cgroup accounting for io_uring against epoll and for `io-tokio` against `io-compio`; the 16-connection json level, which in Round 23 is an environment-wide effect rather than a runtime-shape one: drogon 24,915, nodejs 25,718, h2o 28,981, aspnetcore 26,452, uwebsockets.js 26,284, may-minihttp 27,670, hyper 27,636 and ntex-plt 26,913 all sit between 25K and 30K requests per second, and only libreactor (471,365), lithium (369,744), ntex-plt-compio (276,101) and ntex-compio (264,990) escape it (extraction). The step therefore does not separate zero-core from Drogon and does not decide the accept-distribution strategy; what the harness must explain is the escape, with completion-based receive against readiness wake latency as one hypothesis and the load generator's connection distribution as another, both unverified. The other gates: the 16,384-connection plaintext level with zero errors; the CPU cost per item of a libuv wake and of a batched crossing at the section 8.6 batch sizes; the .NET p99 latency under allocation pressure with the managed-thread-per-core model; the cost of `overflow-checks = true` on the parser hot path; mimalloc against the system allocator inside the three hosts; and the counting-allocator assertion. The HttpArena efficiency methodology that the proposals cite could not be fetched in this task (the README was 404 for the performance judge too) and is unverified; the cgroup CPU-per-request measurement is defined here directly.

## 6. HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3 and QUIC, WebSocket, SSE, TLS

### 6.1 The shared transport abstraction

`zero-http-types` defines the protocol-neutral `RequestHead { method, scheme, authority, path, fields }`, `ResponseHead { status, fields }`, trailers, body chunks, the `Early` marker for 0-RTT and one error enum mapped from the h2 and h3 error spaces. HTTP/3 requests carry the same pseudo-header shape as HTTP/2, and HTTP/1.1 folds `Host` into `:authority`, so three front-end codecs (`zero-http1`, `zero-h2`, `zero-h3`) produce the same values and the router, the handler tiers, the header map, the Date cache, the JSON writer and the database pipeline never learn which transport carried a request (carried from research-http3-and-quic.md section 5). The std seam in `zero-http` is two traits used through generics, never `dyn`, so the h1 hot loop is monomorphized and carries no HTTP/3 dispatch: `StreamTransport { poll_accept_stream, drain(reason), peer() }` and `ByteStream { read(OwnedBuf), write(OwnedBuf), finish, reset(code), stop_sending(code) }`. `reset` and `stop_sending` map to RST_STREAM on HTTP/2 and RESET_STREAM and STOP_SENDING on QUIC and close the connection on HTTP/1.1; `drain` sends GOAWAY with the last accepted stream id on h2 and h3 and sets `Connection: close` on h1. Optional capability traits `Datagrams`, `RawStreams` and `EarlyData` are denied by default and checked by the router so WebTransport and HTTP datagrams stay out of the common path.

### 6.2 HTTP/1.1 codec

`zero-http1` takes a caller-owned buffer and returns a `RequestHead` of byte ranges plus a consumed count, or `Partial`, or `Reject { status, close: true }`; no allocation, a caller-owned header table (64 slots by default, 431 beyond the configured field limit), no clock, no global state, so the parser is a pure function that is fuzzable and never panics (`indexing_slicing`, `arithmetic_side_effects`, `unwrap_used`, `expect_used` and `panic` at deny). Every RFC-permitted ambiguity is rejected rather than normalized, and each rule below is an `http1Parser` vector named after its section. Framing: both Transfer-Encoding and Content-Length are answered with 400 and close (RFC 9112 section 6.1, fetched: a server "MAY reject a request that contains both Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding" and must close the connection afterward); a Transfer-Encoding list whose final element is not `chunked` is 400 and close (section 6.3, fetched: "the server MUST respond with the 400 (Bad Request) status code and then close the connection"); a transfer coding the server does not implement, which is every coding other than `chunked` and includes every obfuscated spelling, is 501 and close, because section 6.1 states that such a server "SHOULD respond with 501 (Not Implemented)" (fetched) and the design follows the SHOULD; chunked on an HTTP/1.0 request is 400 and close; an unsupported major version is 505. Content-Length must match `1*DIGIT` (RFC 9110 section 8.6, fetched); a value that is not `1*DIGIT`, multiple fields with differing values, or a comma-separated list is rejected with 400 and close (the RFC declares the differing and identical-list cases "invalid" framing; the design rejects every list rather than collapsing identical values, and a vector pins that choice). Line ends: a bare LF is rejected, which RFC 9112 section 2.2 permits ("a recipient MAY recognize a single LF as a line terminator", fetched; this parser does not); bare CR, obs-fold, whitespace before the colon, CR, LF or NUL in field values (RFC 9110 section 5.5: "a recipient of CR, LF, or NUL within a field value MUST either reject the message or replace each of those characters with SP", fetched; this parser rejects), and whitespace between the start line and the first field are 400. Request target: the absolute-form is accepted, because "A server MUST accept the absolute-form in requests" (section 3.2.2, fetched), and its authority is the request's authority: "the origin server MUST ignore the received Host header field (if any) and instead use the host information of the request-target" (fetched), so a Host that differs from the absolute-form authority is ignored for routing but recorded, and the route table's `strict_host` option (default on) turns that mismatch into 400; for origin-form a missing, duplicated or invalid Host is 400. Trailers: parsed into a separate table that is never merged into the header section; a trailer that names a framing, routing, request-modifier or authentication field (Host, Content-Length, Transfer-Encoding, Authorization, Cookie, and every field the router or policy reads) is dropped, because "A trailer field MUST NOT be used in a message if the field is defined as a hop-by-hop field, is a request modifier, provides request information, or has frame-altering semantics" (RFC 9110 section 6.5.1, fetched), and handlers reach trailers only through an explicit accessor with an allow list (the rest carried from research-http-and-ws.md section 2). The request-line limit is 8,192 octets because RFC 9112 section 3 recommends "at a minimum, request-line lengths of 8000 octets" (fetched), with 414 for the target and 501 for the method; the other limits are in section 10.4. SIMD scans come from `zero-simd` (32 bytes per AVX2 iteration, 16 per SSE4.2 or NEON, 8 per SWAR word). Drogon's parser scans one byte at a time with `std::find` and `std::equal` (carried from research-http-and-ws.md section 6.4); the design claim is only that this parser does strictly less work per byte, and any speedup is unverified until measured. httparse serves as the differential oracle of the head parser in a `fuzz/` target only (owner decision 2026-10-02, a fuzz-only exception to the 12-month currency rule of `RULES.md`, since httparse 1.10.1 of 2025-03-03 is its newest stable release; crates.io, fetched 2026-10-02); it is no feature of `zero-http1` and never enters a shipped graph, which replaces the earlier `parser-httparse` bring-up feature.

### 6.3 Response serialization, pipelining and the write path

A compile-time status-line table; the per-core Date block; precomputed immutable header blocks per route or static asset (`Server`, `Content-Type`, `Cache-Control`, `ETag`); allocation-free `Content-Length` from a 20-byte stack buffer; one vectored write per event-loop turn with large bodies as separate iovecs; chunked coding for unknown lengths; outbound validation, because the serializer is the response-splitting boundary (RFC 9112 section 11.1, fetched: response splitting "exploits the line-based nature of HTTP message framing and the ordered association of requests to responses on persistent connections"): every field name written by host code must be an RFC 9110 `token` and every value a `field-value` with no CR, LF or NUL and no leading or trailing whitespace, checked once at the accessor (`zero_res_header`, `zero_res_header_id`) so the hot path for precomputed blocks pays nothing, with `InvalidArgument` returned to the handler and the response replaced by a 500 if the handler sends anyway; a `responseSplitting` section in `conformance/vectors.json` is asserted by all three bindings, and the STANDARDS.md statement "a response header whose value contains CR, LF, or NUL is rejected rather than emitted" keeps its row; HEAD, 204, 304 and 1xx bodies suppressed by the serializer regardless of the handler; hop-by-hop fields stripped before h2 or h3 emission. This is the shared technique set of may-minihttp (fixed prefix, itoa lengths, cached date), ntex (static heads, DateService) and actix-server (prebuilt heads) (carried from research-techempower.md sections 4.2 to 4.5). The TechEmpower rules require `Content-Length` or `Transfer-Encoding` on every response and forbid gzip (wiki, fetched), which the serializer satisfies by construction on the benchmark routes.

Pipelining: the read loop parses every complete head in the buffer; each request takes a sequence number in a per-connection in-order ring; responses go out in request order, which RFC 9112 section 9.3 requires (fetched: a server "MUST send the corresponding responses in the same order that the requests were received"); handlers run concurrently only for safe methods and an unsafe method waits for all earlier responses; consecutive ready responses go out in one writev; a rejection marks the connection close and discards the remaining input; unread bodies are drained to a byte budget or the connection closes; in-flight heads are capped at 32 per connection by the codec with a runtime default of 8, leaving excess input in the socket buffer so TCP back pressure applies (carried from research-http-and-ws.md section 10). The plaintext test pipelines at "256, 1024, 4096, and 16,384 concurrency" (wiki, fetched), which is what the ring is sized for.

### 6.4 HTTP/2 (release 2)

In-house sans-I/O `zero-h2` over `zero-hpack`: frames, stream states, flow control capped at 2^31-1, settings validation, CONTINUATION accumulation, GOAWAY, RFC 9218 priority parsing with `SETTINGS_NO_RFC7540_PRIORITIES` advertised, Extended CONNECT for WebSocket, prior-knowledge cleartext for gRPC, no h2c Upgrade. HPACK: 61 static entries, entry cost name plus value plus 32, bounded arena dynamic table, integer limits, Huffman padding rules, never-indexed literals for Authorization, Cookie, Set-Cookie and route-marked fields. Denial-of-service budgets from RFC 9113 section 10.5 with ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM and the h2 crate defaults as starting values (`max_concurrent_streams` 100, `max_frame_size` 16,384, `max_header_list_size` 32,768, `header_table_size` 4,096, the reset-stream limits, `max_send_buffer_size` 400 KiB) plus a sliding window of 200 client resets per 10 s (an unmeasured starting value) against the rapid-reset class (all carried from research-http-and-ws.md section 11 and research-nostd-and-security.md section 12.5; the h2 advisory GHSA-qppj-fm5r-hxr3 was not re-fetched here). h2 and hyper are dev-only interoperability peers, and an `h2-crate` std feature can stand in for HTTP/2 until conformance passes. HTTP/2 is not in release 1 because the yardstick is HTTP/1.1 and it is the largest attack-exposed codec.

### 6.5 HTTP/3 and QUIC

Split. Framing and field compression are in-house no_std codecs; the QUIC transport is adopted. `zero-h3` and `zero-qpack` ship in release 1 as codec crates with conformance vectors and fuzz targets, because they are byte-in, structure-out functions sharing varints, Huffman coding, field validation and limits with the HTTP/2 work. QPACK is static-only at first: RFC 9204 (fetched) gives `SETTINGS_QPACK_MAX_TABLE_CAPACITY` and `SETTINGS_QPACK_BLOCKED_STREAMS` a default of zero, states that with capacity zero "the encoder MUST NOT insert entries into the dynamic table and MUST NOT send any encoder instructions on the encoder stream", and defines a 99-entry static table, so a static-only implementation is complete and conformant with no cross-stream state; dynamic tables are an additive feature after the fuzz corpus has run. `SETTINGS_MAX_FIELD_SECTION_SIZE` is sent explicitly as 32,768 so h1, h2 and h3 accept the same requests.

Crate decision. The transport is quinn-proto (0.11.19, released 2026-09-30, fetched), which "contains no networking code and does not get any relevant timestamps from the operating system", so it is driven by the core's own seam: datagram batches into `Endpoint::handle` and `Connection::handle_event`, `poll_transmit` batches out, the wheel driving `poll_timeout` (carried from research-http3-and-quic.md 4.1). It is configured with `default-features = false, features = ["rustls-aws-lc-rs"]` so the single-provider rule holds; its mandatory graph includes `tracing` 0.1 as a normal dependency (fetched), which is why it sits behind the `http3` cargo feature with its own deny.toml addendum and why the owner decides whether `tracing` is acceptable in the shipped graph (section 18). Rejected: quiche (BoringSSL through cmake, NASM on Windows), s2n-quic (tokio-bound, s2n-tls), neqo (NSS), msquic (C), and an in-house QUIC (quinn-proto alone is 27,528 lines of transport logic and every surveyed stack is six or more years old with 185 to 378 open issues; carried). In-house around the crate: the reactor integration, the connection ID allocator encoding the core index, the eBPF steering program, the 0-RTT policy layer and qlog hooks.

UDP fast path (carried from research-http3-and-quic.md section 3 except where a fetch is named): Linux one `SO_REUSEPORT` UDP socket per core, connection IDs of the form [core index | random], and connection-id based cross-core handoff over the seam's wake as the default steering path: the kernel's reuseport hash lands a datagram on some core, that core reads the core index out of the DCID and forwards the datagram to the owning core by one wake, so every connection stays on one core at the cost of one hop on misrouted datagrams (the fraction is the reuseport hash's miss rate, unmeasured). The `SK_REUSEPORT` eBPF program that steers short-header packets by DCID and long-header packets by 4-tuple hash is an opt-in (`http3.steering = "ebpf"`) because it cannot load where the product will mostly run: loading any BPF program requires `CAP_SYS_ADMIN` or `CAP_BPF` once `unprivileged_bpf_disabled` is 1 or 2, and kernels built with `BPF_UNPRIV_DEFAULT_OFF` default to 2 (docs.kernel.org admin-guide/sysctl/kernel, fetched), while Docker's default seccomp profile denies the `bpf` syscall outright ("Deny loading potentially persistent BPF programs into kernel, already gated by `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`", docs.docker.com, fetched). Its loader is raw `bpf(2)` through `zero-sys` with the program bytecode checked in and a test that loads it on a privileged Linux runner; `zero doctor` reports the program as unavailable in containers and the handoff path as active. Receive through the datagram batch trait with `UDP_GRO`, ECN and pktinfo control messages built and parsed in `zero-sys`, send with `UDP_SEGMENT` (at most 64 datagrams per call) and per-packet ECN, `IP_PMTUDISC_PROBE` and `IP_RECVERR` for DPLPMTUD, a 1,452-byte upper bound. Windows HTTP/3 is functional only in release 3: one socket, no GSO, no GRO (`UDP_RECV_MAX_COALESCED_SIZE` stays off while quinn issue 2041, "Potential bug in GRO code for Windows?", opened 2024-11-14, is open; fetched), ECN best effort, no per-core steering, one recvfrom per datagram through tokio's `UdpSocket`, because `UDP_SEND_MSG_SIZE`, ECN and pktinfo on Windows need `WSASendMsg` and `WSARecvMsg` with control messages that tokio's `UdpSocket` does not expose; Windows UDP offload is a feature of the `io-compio` backend, where `WSASendMsg` is native, and is excluded from the promotion criteria below. macOS one recvmsg per datagram with `IP_RECVTOS`, development grade.

Alt-Svc. RFC 7838 (fetched) defines `Alt-Svc = clear / 1#alt-value`, the `ma` parameter in seconds with a 24-hour default, `persist=1`, and requires that clients "MUST have reasonable assurances that the alternative service is under control of and valid for the whole origin". Alt-Svc emission is off by default: a UDP self-probe on the same host cannot see the external firewall or the container port mapping that risk 14 describes, and a false positive sends clients to a blocked UDP path. The core emits `Alt-Svc: h3=":<udp-port>"; ma=86400` on h1 and h2 responses only when the operator sets `http3.advertise = true` (an explicit statement that UDP reaches the listener from outside) or supplies `http3.probe_from = "<address>"`, an external checker that the core asks to reach its UDP port before advertising, and only while a QUIC listener is bound with the same certificate (never a different host, never `persist=1`); it emits `Alt-Svc: clear` for one `ma` period after disabling, and `zero doctor` prints the operator DNS line `HTTPS 1 . alpn="h3,h2"`.

0-RTT policy. RFC 8470 (fetched) defines `Early-Data: 1`, the 425 (Too Early) status ("the server is unwilling to risk processing a request that might be replayed"), and gives a server three options: reject early data at the TLS layer, delay processing until the handshake completes, or send 425. The default is the first (rustls `max_early_data_size` 0). When enabled per listener: streams marked `Early`, only safe methods on routes flagged `early_data`, everything else deferred until handshake completion, 425 when an `Early-Data: 1` header arrives from an intermediary, and the proxy middleware forwards `Early-Data` as the RFC requires of intermediaries. Passive migration and NAT rebinding from the start, no `preferred_address`, 20 s keep-alive default on QUIC listeners, server push rejected on every protocol, transport limits as in section 10.4.

Release. Codecs in release 1; `zero-quic` and the h3 adapter in release 3, compiled into published binaries under `http3` and runtime-off (`listen({ http3: false })`). Promotion to default-on on Linux requires the interop runner cases (handshake, transfer, retry, resumption, ecn, keyupdate, http3) against the implementations the runner registers as Docker images through `implementations_quic.json`, quic-go and ngtcp2 among them (the runner README lists no browser client; fetched), a separate headless-browser check in which Chrome and Firefox load an h3 page after receiving Alt-Svc and the harness asserts the second load used h3 (about 2 days, section 16), a CPU-per-request measurement of the QUIC path with GSO, GRO and ack frequency inside the Fastly parity band with TLS over TCP, and NAT-rebinding tests of the steering fallback (carried from research-http3-and-quic.md sections 6 and 8). HTTP/3 moves no TechEmpower number: the toolset drives HTTP/1.1 and has no HTTP/3 test (carried from research-techempower.md section 6), so it is a product and tail-latency feature and must never add dispatch to the h1 loop.

### 6.6 WebSocket and SSE

`zero-ws` validates the handshake in the h1 layer (GET, `Upgrade: websocket`, version 13, 16-byte key, Origin hook), computes the accept value with SHA-1 from `zero-server-crypto` into a 28-byte stack buffer through `zero-base64::encode_slice`, decodes frames over the caller buffer with the minimal-length rule, RSV bits zero unless permessage-deflate was negotiated, control frames unfragmented and at most 125 bytes, unmasked client frames closed with 1002, no interleaved fragments, validated close codes, streaming UTF-8 validation across fragments, in-place SIMD unmask so delivery is zero-copy, a 16 MiB default message cap, fragment and control-frame budgets, permessage-deflate feature-gated and off by default (all carried from research-http-and-ws.md section 12). The three Node audit bugs (head bytes lost after upgrade, continuation frames dropped, write after close) become conformance vectors. Rooms and pools live in `zero-realtime` with cross-core fan-out through the seam's wakes.

`zero-sse` writes `event:`, `id:`, `retry:` and one `data:` line per LF-separated line, rejects ids with NUL at the API, sends one chunk per event with an immediate flush over h1 and one DATA frame per event over h2, a `:` keep-alive comment every 15 s unless an event was sent, exposes Last-Event-ID to the handler, and provides a client decoder for `zero-fetch` (carried from research-http-and-ws.md section 13).

### 6.7 TLS

rustls 0.23.45 (docs.rs, fetched: aws-lc-rs is the default provider; a provider is either installed process-wide with `install_default()` or provided explicitly when building a `ServerConfig`; features `std`, `aws_lc_rs`, `ring`, `fips`, `prefer-post-quantum`, `custom-provider`, `tls12`, `logging`, `read_buf`, `brotli`, `zlib`), moving to 0.24 with `rustls-aws-lc-rs` and `rustls-ring` when released. The library never calls `install_default()`, because it is loaded into Node, Python and .NET hosts that may own the process-wide provider; it takes an `Arc<CryptoProvider>` through `builder_with_provider`. `default-features = false`; `logging` off in release; aws-lc-rs on the tier-one targets (X25519MLKEM768, FIPS behind a feature never on in bindings), ring behind a feature for no_std, wasm and toolchain-constrained builds. Measured graphs (measure-cargo-tree.txt, cargo 1.96.0, 2026-09-29, with tokio and tokio-rustls included in that measurement although this design uses neither): 25 crates with build edges and 15 with normal edges for aws-lc-rs plus std plus tls12 on Linux; 20 and 19 with ring on Linux and Windows; 16 with ring and no std.

`zero-tls` drives rustls over the seam with owned buffers through two drivers, so tokio-rustls is not a dependency and the TLS layer moves with the backend: the buffered `ServerConnection` API on `io-tokio`, and the unbuffered API on `io-compio`, which is a separate state-machine driver (rustls's `unbuffered` module: `UnbufferedConnectionCommon`, `UnbufferedStatus`, `ConnectionState`, `EncodeTlsData`, `TransmitTlsData` and the other state types, with no std traits; fetched by the feasibility review) and is priced as its own line in section 16 because both backends run the full test matrix in release 1. Shipped `ServerConfig` (carried from research-tls-and-deps.md section 5 except where a fetch is named): TLS 1.3 and 1.2, provider suite defaults with AES-256-GCM first and `ignore_client_order = true`, ALPN `h2` then `http/1.1` (`http/1.1` alone when HTTP/2 is off), `max_early_data_size = 0` and `send_half_rtt_data = false` (both the rustls 0.23.45 defaults; fetched), `require_ems = true` whenever TLS 1.2 is enabled, because rustls defaults it to true only under a FIPS provider and false otherwise (docs.rs ServerConfig, fetched) and a TLS 1.2 session without the RFC 7627 extended master secret is not a "maximum security" default; an operator may set it to false for a named legacy client population and the option's documentation records that this is the one TLS 1.2 downgrade the product allows. `TicketRotator` with 6 h generation and 12 h acceptance, session cache 256 entries configurable to 0, certificate compression off, `enable_secret_extraction` only on kTLS listeners. rustls has no handshake timeout or handshake-count field (ServerConfig page, fetched), so `zero-limits` carries `tls_handshake_timeout` (10 s from the first byte to the handshake's completion) and a per-core cap on in-progress handshakes (1,024 by default), enforced by the connection driver, so a client cannot hold half-open handshakes before the 30 s header timeout starts. Certificates through `rustls_pki_types::pem`, `ResolvesServerCert` for SNI with an atomic `Arc<CertifiedKey>` swap and `keys_match` validation, a default identity for unknown SNI, optional mTLS through `WebPkiClientVerifier` with the builder's CRL and revocation options exposed as `client_auth.crls` and `client_auth.revocation` and recorded as a registry row (the builder page was not fetched in this task, so the exact method names are unverified). Private keys are supplied as a file path or as a host byte buffer that the facade zeroizes after the call returns, never as a host string, because a host string cannot be zeroized. The in-house OCSP stapler fetches through `zero-fetch` and accepts a response only after the six RFC 6960 section 3.2 checks (fetched): the CertID in the response matches the served certificate, the signature is valid, the signer's identity matches, the signer is currently authorized (the issuer's key, or a responder certificate carrying id-kp-OCSPSigning issued directly by that issuer, section 4.2.2.2, fetched; the "trusted responder" option is not implemented), thisUpdate is sufficiently recent, and nextUpdate is in the future; signature and chain checks run through rustls-webpki and the provider, the AIA fetch itself may be plaintext HTTP as the protocol allows because the response is signed, an unverifiable response leaves the last good staple in place and raises a counter, refresh happens at half the remaining interval, and a must-staple certificate refuses to start with stapling off; the DER walker and the OCSP response parser are a libFuzzer target (`zero-tls ocsp_der`) with vectors from RFC 6960 and one conformance row per acceptance requirement. kTLS in house on Linux (opt-in per listener, AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 only, drain at a record boundary, control-record and TLS 1.3 KeyUpdate handling, `TLS_TX_ZEROCOPY_RO` only for static-file sendfile, user-space fallback exercised in CI; carried from research-tls-and-deps.md section 4) with every `setsockopt` and `crypto_info` struct in `zero-sys`. Option names mirror `lib/app.js` and `lib/fetch` (`allowHTTP1`, `minVersion`, `maxVersion`, `servername`, `ciphers`) so the Node facade keeps its shape, and the ALPN, h2-over-TLS and 0-RTT conformance statements in STANDARDS.md carry over unchanged. On QUIC, `rustls::quic::ServerConnection` reuses the same resolver, ticketer and staple, with `h3` added to the ALPN list on the QUIC listener only (carried from research-http3-and-quic.md, rustls quic module).

## 7. Router and handler model

### 7.1 Router

`zero-router` is a no_std matcher over integer method ids: static segments, parameters, wildcards, 404, 405 with `Allow`, 501, automatic HEAD for GET and OPTIONS, RFC 3986 dot-segment removal, percent-decoding that returns an error instead of panicking (the Node audit's URIError crash), router-level middleware and query-string mounts with the semantics and tests transferred from zero-server's router suite (carried from salvage-map.md section 2.3). Routes are values, so the matcher resolves a handler descriptor rather than a closure, and a tier 0 route completes inside the matcher's caller without a handler frame. The Node router it replaces is a linear regex scan measured at 10.9 microseconds per miss with 400 routes (carried from salvage-map.md section 2.7); the new matcher must beat that by construction, which is unverified until measured.

### 7.2 Five handler tiers

Ordered so that everything expressible as data runs in Rust without a boundary crossing (carried from research-bindings-and-handlers.md section 6, with the binding-first boundary rules applied):

- Tier 0, declarative routes: static bodies, files and directories, redirects, health and readiness probes, proxy targets, and rejections (rate limit, missing or invalid JWT, CORS preflight, body too large, CSRF failure). The bound language builds the value once; `zero-policy` and `zero-static` own matching, conditional requests, compression policy and the write path. Zero crossings.
- Tier 1, cached handlers: a handler registered with a key specification (path, selected query keys, selected headers, principal id from the verified JWT), a TTL, a stale-while-revalidate window and invalidation tags. Hits are served from the per-core `zero-cache` shard with no cross-thread lock; misses fall through to tier 3; `cache.invalidate(tag)` is one broadcast off the request path.
- Tier 2, data routes: the bound language registers a `QueryPlan` (parameterized SQL text or a `zero-sql` AST) with parameter bindings from path, query, claims, validated body fields, constants or a random range, plus a serialization shape (object, array, scalar, or a `zero-template` id) and validation rules. Rust pipelines the statements on the worker's connection and serializes binary columns straight into the response buffer. This tier carries db, query, updates, fortunes and cached queries for every binding with no host code on the request path. Off the request path, the same executor backs the Node, Python and C# ORM facades through an async call (Promise, awaitable, `ValueTask`), where the 1.8 microsecond pipelined Promise cost measured in section 2 is acceptable.
- Tier 3, batched bound-language handlers: ready requests queue per core; the dispatcher in `zero-rt` hands each batch (whatever is ready, capped at 256) to the host target paired with that core, with a bounded number of batches in flight per target (4 by default) and the back-pressure rule of section 8.5 when the target is full. The batch size is whatever the core has ready, because the measurements show the per-item cost falls with items in flight at the target rather than with batch size (8 items with 8 batches in flight cost 187 ns per item against 2,218 ns with one in flight; section 2), so the dispatcher never holds a ready request back to grow a batch. Sync handlers run on the target's thread (a Node isolate, the Python handler thread, a managed .NET thread), never on the I/O worker; the worker keeps serving tiers 0 to 2 while the host runs the batch. A handler returning "next" is middleware; middleware that only inspects headers or claims is expressed as tier 0 rules instead. Errors thrown by handlers map to the transferred zero-server error registry inside Rust, so the error path never crosses twice.
- Tier 4, Rust: in-process `async fn` handlers registered on the request and response types directly as `!Send` futures polled inline by the owning connection task (section 5.6), with `spawn_local` available to a handler that wants detached work; this is the TechEmpower entry and the Drogon-class path. A dynamic form exposes a versioned `#[repr(C)]` vtable (`zero_plugin_abi_version`, `zero_plugin_register`) with the same opaque `ZeroRequest` and `ZeroResponse` handles and accessor functions the .NET binding consumes, generated once by cbindgen; it stays on the C ABI because a stable Rust ABI across compiler versions is not something this task verified. The loader ships only with the trust model of section 10.8.

Ordering across tiers: safe methods may run in parallel and responses leave in request order through the per-connection ring of section 6.3; a tier 3 batch therefore carries requests from many connections and completion order within the batch is free.

### 7.3 Request views and bodies

A request is a 53-bit slot id into the per-worker arena from parse to final write, never a per-request finalizable object (section 8.3). Accessors return integers and borrowed byte views by default and decode strings on demand with memoization in the arena; common header names are interned integer ids. The response builder is addressed by the same slot: `status`, `header(name_id, value)`, `body_bytes`, `body_str`, `json`, `file`, `sse_open`, `ws_accept`, `send`.

Slot ownership across threads. Host threads (a Node isolate, the Python handler thread, a .NET thread-pool thread continuing a `ValueTask`) call `zero_req_*` and `zero_res_*` on memory the worker thread owns and recycles, so the slot lifecycle is an explicit state machine held in one atomic word per slot in `zero-rt` (safe Rust; atomics need no `unsafe`), not a convention:

- States: `Free`, `Parsing`, `WorkerOwned`, `Leased { generation, readers }`, `Completing`, `Closed`. Only the worker moves a slot into `Leased` (when it dispatches the batch) and out of `Completing` (when it writes the response).
- Every accessor performs a compare-and-swap borrow: it reads the word, checks the generation against the id, requires the state to be `Leased`, increments `readers`, performs the read or write, and decrements on return. A generation mismatch or a state other than `Leased` returns `Closed` without touching the slot. The generation check and the memory access are therefore one protected critical section, not two separate operations.
- `zero_batch_complete` moves the slot to `Completing` with a release store; the worker acquires it, refuses to recycle any slot whose `readers` is nonzero (it re-polls that slot on the next turn and counts a `late_reader` metric), writes the response, and only then moves the slot to `Free` and bumps the generation.
- A leased slot has its own response buffer, allocated from the arena when the slot is leased and separate from the per-core write slab; the worker never touches it until `Completing`. The worker may set a cancel flag on a leased slot (client went away, timeout) but never frees it; connection close while a slot is leased defers the free until completion or the lease timeout (the request total timeout of section 10.4), after which the slot moves to `Closed` and every later accessor returns `Closed`.
- The arena is chunked with stable addresses: chunks are added, never reallocated, so a borrowed view handed to a host never dangles because the arena grew.
- `zero-ffi` never dereferences arena memory without holding a borrow token from this protocol, which is a lint-checked invariant (every accessor is written through one `with_slot` helper) and the subject of a loom model and a TSan job that race a late accessor against recycle and run tier 0 traffic and tier 3 completions on the same core concurrently.
- Index reuse is epoch-based in addition to the generation: a freed index is not handed out again until every registered host target has acknowledged the completion epoch in which it was freed (targets acknowledge with each `zero_batch_complete`), so a stale id held by a slow host cannot collide with a live request even before the 30-bit generation would wrap (about 3 hours at 1e5 reuses per second on one index, against 21 seconds with the 21-bit layout the design carried before this revision).

Bodies. A request body view is borrowed only where the host type system enforces the borrow: .NET `ReadOnlySpan<byte>` inside a `ref struct`, and PyO3 `&[u8]` converted to `bytes` before the call returns. In Node, napi's `BufferSlice` binds only the Rust side to the callback scope ("the lifetime is bound to the fn closure", docs.rs, fetched); the `Buffer` object handed to JavaScript can be stored and read after the slot is recycled, and the only zero-copy constructor, `from_external`, is `unsafe` and documents that "JavaScript may mutate the data passed in to this buffer" (fetched), which would make the parser's byte ranges writable from JavaScript. So `zero_req_body` in Node always returns a JavaScript-owned copy (`copy_from`), `zero_req_body_retain` is an alias of it, and the Node budget in section 8.6 includes that copy. Response bodies are copied into Rust-owned buffers below 64 KiB. Above it, ownership is inverted rather than shared: `zero_res_body_alloc(slot, len)` returns a Rust-owned region that the host fills and `zero_res_send` seals; in Node the region is exposed as an external `ArrayBuffer` over a pooled per-isolate staging area (one finalizer per pool region, never per request) and `zero_res_send` detaches it so no live JavaScript view survives the send (`napi_detach_arraybuffer` is in the Node-API index; its text could not be retrieved in this task and the detach behavior is unverified until the smoke test asserts that a view read after send throws or reads zero bytes); in .NET the host writes through a `Span<byte>` over the region inside a `ref struct` that cannot escape the call; in Python the region is a writable `memoryview` released by the facade at send. A host that mutates a buffer after send therefore changes nothing on the wire, and a conformance vector detaches or mutates after send and asserts the response bytes are unchanged. `zero_res_body_transfer(slot, ptr, len, release_fn)` remains only for buffers the binding pins for the whole queue lifetime (a .NET `GCHandle` pinned until `release_fn`, a Python `Py_buffer` held until `release_fn`) and is not offered to Node at all, because an `ArrayBuffer` can be detached by `ArrayBuffer.prototype.transfer` ("creates a new `ArrayBuffer` with the same byte content as this buffer, then detaches this buffer", MDN, fetched) while the worker's writev is queued, and whether Node marks its own `Buffer` backing stores as non-detachable is unverified.

## 8. Binding model for TypeScript, Python and C#

### 8.1 One C ABI, generated once

`zero-ffi` exports the curated C ABI, cbindgen generates `include/zero.h` on every build inside the workspace checkout (the pamoja build.rs), and the three bindings mirror it: napi-rs functions, PyO3 functions and `[LibraryImport]` declarations. The accessor surface, adopted verbatim from the binding-first proposal as every judge asked:

- Request reads, all taking the slot id, passing through the borrow protocol of section 7.3, and returning integers or views: `zero_req_method` (u8 enum), `zero_req_path`, `zero_req_query`, `zero_req_param(slot, index)` (index from the route's parameter table), `zero_req_header_id(slot, name_id)` over the generated interned-name table, `zero_req_header(slot, name_ptr, name_len)` for the long tail, `zero_req_trailer(slot, name_ptr, name_len)` over the separate trailer table with its allow list, `zero_req_body(slot)` (a borrowed view in .NET and Python, a copy in Node), `zero_req_body_retain(slot)` (one copy into a language-owned buffer), `zero_req_claim(slot, name)` (claims already verified in Rust), `zero_req_peer(slot)` (address, scheme, ALPN, transport kind). Release 2 adds `zero_req_body_read(slot, buf, len)` for incremental reads above the buffered threshold, paired with a body-chunk event on the batch path.
- Response writes, each validating its arguments and returning `InvalidArgument` rather than emitting: `zero_res_status(slot, u16)` (100 to 599 only), `zero_res_header_id(slot, name_id, value)` and `zero_res_header(slot, name, value)` (name must be an RFC 9110 token; value must contain no CR, LF or NUL and no leading or trailing whitespace; section 6.3), `zero_res_body_copy(slot, bytes)` for bodies under 64 KiB, `zero_res_body_alloc(slot, len)` returning the Rust-owned region of section 7.3 for larger bodies, `zero_res_body_transfer(slot, ptr, len, release_fn)` for pinned host buffers in .NET and Python only, `zero_res_json(slot, bytes)`, `zero_res_file(slot, path)` (the path goes through the `zero-static` policy: every segment checked, no traversal, `O_NOFOLLOW` or canonicalize-and-compare, the Windows colon and short-name rules), `zero_res_sse_open(slot)`, `zero_res_ws_accept(slot)`, then `zero_res_send(slot)`. Release 2 adds `zero_res_write(slot, chunk)` and `zero_res_end(slot)` over the chunked encoder, with `zero_res_writable(slot)` as the backpressure query.
