- WebSocket and SSE after the upgrade or open, addressed by a connection id rather than a slot: a `ws` event batch descriptor (connection id, opcode, payload view, close code and reason) delivered through the same batch dispatcher, `zero_ws_send(conn, opcode, ptr, len)`, `zero_ws_close(conn, code, reason_ptr, reason_len)`, `zero_ws_writable(conn)` plus a `drained` event when a full send queue empties, `zero_ws_ping(conn)` with pong delivered as an event; `zero_sse_send(conn, event, id, data)`, `zero_sse_close(conn)`, `zero_sse_writable(conn)`; `zero_room_join(conn, room)`, `zero_room_leave(conn, room)`, `zero_room_broadcast(room, opcode, ptr, len)` over `zero-realtime`. Payload views obey the same rule as request bodies (borrowed in .NET and Python, a copy in Node). These ship in release 1 with `ws` and `sse` sections in `conformance/vectors.json`, because `app.ws` and `res.sse` are release 1 facade features and a binding cannot implement them from `zero_res_ws_accept` alone.
- Batch completion: `zero_batch_complete(worker, slots_ptr, count, epoch)` posts one wake to the owning worker per batch and acknowledges the completion epoch of section 7.3; facades accumulate completed slots and flush at the end of the batch iteration (sync handlers) or from a scheduled microtask or continuation (async handlers).
- Lifecycle: `zero_server_start`, `zero_server_shutdown`, route and policy registration, `zero_last_error_message`, `ZeroStatus` (`Ok = 0`, Protocol, Io, Codec, Closed, Auth, Unsupported, Timeout, Limit, InvalidArgument, Panic), `*_free` for every owned handle.
- Every accessor is total: null pointers, stale slots and out-of-range indexes return a status, never a panic across the boundary; every export runs under `catch_unwind` and reports `Panic`, since unwinding across `extern "C"` is undefined behavior and the ANSSI guide's FFI-NOPANIC rule ("Handle `panic!` correctly in FFI") and FFI-CTYPE ("Use only C-compatible types in FFI"), FFI-CAPI ("Expose dedicated C-compatible API only") and FFI-MEM-OWNER ("Ensure clear data ownership in FFI") rules apply (rule ids from the ANSSI checklist, fetched).

### 8.2 Batch descriptor and dispatcher

A batch is one `#[repr(C)]` struct: worker index, count, a pointer to a slot-id array, a pointer to a parallel route-id array (so the facade dispatches to the right handler without reading the path), the completion epoch, and a flags word (early data, upgrade request, ws event batch). Node receives it through one ThreadsafeFunction call per batch on the isolate paired with the worker; Python through one post to the facade's handler thread; .NET through one `[UnmanagedCallersOnly]` call on the managed thread paired with the worker. The dispatcher sends whatever is ready up to 256 per batch and keeps at most 4 batches in flight per target; when a target is full the batch stays queued on the worker, the worker stops reading from the connections that fed it (TCP back pressure), and past a per-core bound on queued batches (16 by default) new tier 3 requests on that core are answered 503 with `Retry-After` from tier 0 (section 8.5 gives the per-language mechanism; section 7.2 the measured reason for not holding requests back to grow a batch).

### 8.3 Slot ids

7 bits worker index (128 workers), 30 bits generation, 16 bits arena index (65,536 slots per worker, which at the 1M-connection gate on 56 workers is 17,858 connections per worker with room for pipelined requests): 53 bits so the id survives as a JavaScript number without BigInt. The layout the design carried before this revision (8, 21 and 24 bits) let a hot index wrap its generation in about 21 seconds at 1e5 reuses per second; 30 bits raises that to about 3 hours, and the epoch-based reuse rule of section 7.3 removes the dependence on the wrap period altogether. A stale id (generation mismatch, or a state other than `Leased`) makes every accessor return `Closed` rather than another request's data, and the check and the access are one critical section under the borrow protocol. Each Node isolate keeps a small pool of reusable view objects whose `slot` field is set per request, because creating one finalizable object per request costs 826 ns in Node (section 2); Python may allocate a `#[pyclass]` view per request (196 ns measured) but the facade still pools; .NET receives a `#[repr(C)]` view struct by pointer (1.3 ns fill measured).

### 8.4 Thread ownership and signals

The core spawns its workers in every host through one `zero_server_start`: the napi addon, the PyO3 module, the .NET cdylib and the standalone binary all call it. Handler targets are the Node isolates (one per core by default), the Python facade's handler thread pool and the .NET managed thread per core; none of them is an I/O thread, and no I/O worker ever attaches to a host runtime. The core never installs signal handlers inside a host process; the bindings wire Node process signals, the Python `signal` module and .NET `PosixSignalRegistration` to `zero_server_shutdown`. The Node facade keeps `clusterize` as a compatibility shim that forwards to the `threads` option.

### 8.5 Per language

- TypeScript (Node): a process-global core with one isolate per core as the default deployment. `app.listen()` on the main thread spawns a `worker_threads` pool sized to `os.availableParallelism()` (overridable with `threads`), each worker running the same entry module; each isolate loads the context-aware addon, keeps per-isolate state with `napi_set_instance_data`, registers its own ThreadsafeFunction and unregisters it in an env cleanup hook, because napi.rs documents that "you can't access `napi_env`, `napi_value`, and `napi_ref` on another thread" (fetched), and is pinned to one Rust worker: batches from worker k go to isolate k only, so no request crosses cores and section 5.1's rule holds without an aggregation queue. This is the 56-JavaScript-thread shape of the uwebsockets.js entry (one cluster worker per CPU; fetched), which is the yardstick; the difference that remains is the ThreadsafeFunction hop, whose wall cost at the json test's 9 in flight per core is 1 to 2 microseconds per request (section 2) and whose CPU cost is a section 5.7 gate. Handler tables are per isolate and keyed by route id: the first isolate to register defines the process-global Rust route table, every later isolate must register an identical table (compared by hash of the route descriptors) or `app.listen()` fails with the differing route named, and the dispatcher sends a batch only to an isolate that registered a handler for every route id in it, which the identical-table rule makes true by construction. One ThreadsafeFunction call per batch in the `NonBlocking` mode with `CalleeHandled: false` (napi.rs, fetched: `NonBlocking` returns `QueueFull` rather than waiting, and `CalleeHandled: false` passes the value directly without an error-first pair), created with `max_queue_size` 4 so the queue is bounded (the Node-API text for the size-0 unbounded default was not retrieved in this task; the napi.rs page was); on `QueueFull` the batch stays queued on the worker, the worker stops reading from the connections that fed it, dispatch to that isolate pauses until a `zero_batch_complete` arrives, and past 16 queued batches the core answers new tier 3 requests with 503 and `Retry-After` (section 8.2). The ThreadsafeFunction is unreferenced (`napi_unref_threadsafe_function`) when the server closes so the process can exit. JavaScript iterates slot ids through the pooled view object, calls the user handler, writes through sync accessors and pushes the slot onto a completion array flushed by one `zero_batch_complete`; a Promise-returning handler completes later through the same sync path plus a microtask-scheduled flush; Rust never awaits a JavaScript Promise. Every handler invocation runs inside a try/catch that maps the thrown value to the error registry before the slot is completed, so an exception never reaches the addon boundary. Integer arguments go through pamoja's `Whole<T>` checker. Release 2 carries an inline-loop experiment that removes the hop entirely: the isolate's thread hosts its Rust worker, the runtime's poll descriptor is registered with that thread's libuv loop, and the handler is a same-thread call as in uWebSockets.js; it ships only if the harness row that runs the json test through a Node handler shows it ahead of the ThreadsafeFunction model, and that row runs against uwebsockets.js from the archived tree before any Node yardstick claim is made. `napi = { version = "3", default-features = false, features = ["napi6"] }`, no `tokio_rt` (the core owns its threads); the measured graph with `default-features = false` is 32 crates, mostly proc-macro tooling (carried from research-tls-and-deps.md section 2). Facade: `createApp`, `app.get("/health", ok())`, `files("./public", { etag: true })`, `query("select ... where id = $1", { params: ["path.id"], shape: "object" })`, `cached({ ttl: "30s", key: ["path", "auth.sub"] }, handler)`, plain `(req, res)` handlers, `app.ws`, `app.listen({ port, tls, http2, http3 })`, Model classes over the tier 2 executor, error classes over the transferred registry.
- Python: an I/O worker never attaches to the interpreter. `Python::attach` "Acquires the global interpreter lock" and creates a thread state for a thread that has none (docs.rs pyo3, fetched), so a worker that attached with a pending batch would block its whole event loop, every connection on that core included, until the GIL freed, which contradicts goal 2. The facade owns a handler thread pool instead: one thread under the GIL (N threads on free-threaded builds, N configurable), each attached once for its lifetime, fed by one SPSC batch queue per worker; workers post batches and continue serving tiers 0 to 2, sync handlers run on the handler thread through a `#[pyclass]` view whose slot is reset per request (36 ns per attached call measured, section 2; the attach-per-call figure of 2,219 ns is what the pool avoids), and completions come back through `zero_batch_complete` exactly as for Node. The asyncio loop runs on that same handler thread, so `async def` handlers and sync handlers share one attach and one `call_soon_threadsafe` per batch, and each coroutine completes through a sync call into Rust; the documentation states that sync handlers are the fast path. Every handler invocation runs inside a `try` that maps the exception to the error registry before completion, so no Python exception reaches the Rust boundary. Under the GIL this is one handler thread for the process; the measured 36 ns is the uncontended figure, and a contention benchmark (8 and 56 producer workers posting into one GIL thread) is a section 8.6 harness row whose result replaces the provisional Python budget. PyO3's `experimental-async` is not used because its futures must be `Send + 'static` and stay attached to the interpreter while polled (pyo3.rs async-await page, fetched). Packaging: `abi3-py310` wheels for GIL builds, and version-specific wheels for free-threaded 3.13t and later, because "there is not yet an equivalent to the limited API for the free-threaded ABI" and PyO3 ignores abi3 there with a warning (pyo3.rs free-threading page, fetched); modules are assumed thread-safe by default from PyO3 0.28 (`gil_used = true` is the opt-out, fetched). `pyo3 = { version = "0.29", features = ["abi3-py310"] }` with its measured 13-crate graph; pyo3-stub-gen dev-only; pyo3-async-runtimes only if the asyncio bridge cannot be written over `call_soon_threadsafe` alone (open question, section 18). Free-threaded scaling is unverified (no 3.13t interpreter was available for the probes).
- C#: `DisableRuntimeMarshalling` assembly-wide, `AllowUnsafeBlocks`, `[LibraryImport]` with UTF-8 or byte spans and never `string` on the hot path (the decode is 18.0 ns against a 4.5 ns crossing); `[LibraryImport]` is the .NET 7 source-generated P/Invoke whose marshalling is generated at compile time and can be inlined, while `DllImport` IL stubs "aren't available for ahead-of-time (AOT) compiler or IL trimming scenarios" (learn.microsoft.com, fetched). `[SuppressGCTransition]` only on trivial view accessors, because Microsoft's conditions are that the native function executes in under a microsecond, performs no blocking syscall, does not call back into the runtime, does not throw and does not touch locks, with GC starvation, immediate runtime termination and data corruption as the consequences of misuse, and because the attribute "can cause the P/Invoke export to be bound earlier as a side-effect of the calling method being JIT compiled" (fetched); therefore `NativeLibrary.SetDllImportResolver` is registered in a module initializer before any such method can be compiled (the early-binding `DllNotFoundException` was reproduced in the research probes; carried). Function pointers rooted for the process lifetime, `SafeHandle` per pamoja `NativeHandle.cs`, `GCHandle` for the dispatch context, one `[UnmanagedCallersOnly]` dispatch per batch. Handlers never run inline on the I/O worker: running managed code on the worker would make each core's event loop a managed thread for the duration of the call, so a garbage-collection suspension or a handler that blocks would stall every connection on that core (the mechanics of GC suspension during reverse P/Invoke were not fetched in this task and are unverified; the design does not depend on them either way). Instead the facade pairs each worker with one managed thread (a dedicated `Thread`, not the pool) that blocks on the worker's batch queue, runs sync handlers, and completes through `zero_batch_complete`; the worker posts the batch and continues. The 2.7 ns reverse P/Invoke after a one-time 11,100 ns attach (measured) is what the managed thread pays per batch, not per request; the inline reverse call is kept only for the trivial view accessors, which do no allocation. `ValueTask` handlers continue on the thread pool and complete through a function pointer; the documentation names the `ValueTask` path as the default for anything that does I/O and states that sync handlers must not block. The dispatch stub wraps the batch in try/catch that maps any exception to a `ZeroStatus` and completes the slot with 500, so a managed exception never escapes `[UnmanagedCallersOnly]`. The section 5.7 gate records p99 latency under allocation pressure with this model before the 0.70 to 0.90 band of section 8.8 is advertised. Request type is a `ref struct` over the view; response bodies below 64 KiB copied, above it through `zero_res_body_alloc` written by a `Span<byte>` inside the `ref struct`, and `zero_res_body_transfer` only with a `GCHandle` pinned until `release_fn`. Facade in minimal-API style: `app.MapGet("/users/{id}", Query.Object("..."))`, `Func<Request, Response>` handlers.

### 8.6 FFI cost budget

Per-request boundary cost on tier 3, from the measurements in section 2 (Windows desktop wall time; provisional until the Linux rerun of section 12.5). Node: the crossing cost depends on items in flight at the isolate, so the budget is a table rather than one number, each entry the measured crossing plus one pooled view reset, three to five sync accessor calls at about 12 ns each, and the request body copy when a body is read: at 1 item and 1 batch in flight 19,500 ns (the light-load case, where latency is the only thing at stake); at 4 items and 4 in flight 700 ns; at 8 items and 8 in flight 250 ns; at 16 items and 2 or more in flight 200 ns; at 64 or more items 150 ns. The json test at 512 connections on 56 cores sits in the 4-to-9-items region, so the Node tier 3 budget that matters for the yardstick is 700 ns of wall time per request, and the CPU share of it is the gate. Python: 16 ns per batched item plus accessors at 33 to 55 ns each, budget 150 ns uncontended, to be replaced by the contended figure of the section 8.5 benchmark. .NET: 2.7 ns per batch plus 1.3 ns view fills and 3.0 to 4.5 ns per accessor, budget 25 ns. Anything that would push a request over its budget (a Promise per request at 1,836 ns, a finalizable object per request at 826 ns, a per-request thread hop instead of a batch, a per-call Python attach at 2,219 ns, a `string` marshal on the .NET hot path) is a design defect, and the bench crate carries a per-binding micro-harness that measures each (batch, in-flight) cell and fails when a cell exceeds its budget. Tiers 0 to 2 have a boundary budget of zero on the request path.

### 8.7 The contract tier and what release 1 ships

Three generated declaration sets, one contract: the cbindgen header, the napi-rs `index.d.ts` plus the TypeScript facade (`tsc -b`), and the PyO3 stub written by the `stub_gen` binary; `[LibraryImport]` declarations mirror the header one to one. `conformance/api-surface.json`, generated once from zero-server's JSDoc (238 exports; carried from salvage-map.md section 2.4), gives every export a canonical id and a kind (`ffi`, `facade`, `host-only`), and each binding carries a mapping file from canonical id to its own name (snake_case in the header and the PyO3 stub, camelCase in `index.d.ts`, PascalCase in the `[LibraryImport]` declarations and the C# facade) and shape; CI diffs by canonical id, so a missing export or a changed parameter list fails the build without a literal name comparison across conventions, and `host-only` entries (Model classes, error classes) are checked by a per-binding export test rather than by the header diff. `conformance/vectors.json` gains the sections `http1Parser`, `router`, `jwt`, `cookies`, `rateLimit`, `qpack` and `h3Frames` from release 1 and is asserted by all three bindings. Release 1 ships the generated header, a .NET smoke test that loads the cdylib and runs the conformance vectors, and a Python smoke import over the same cdylib, even though the full Python and C# facades follow in release 2, so that three language hosts can load the first release; the free-threaded wheel matrix is decided at that point.

### 8.8 Expected relative throughput per tier (judgment)

Relative to a tier 4 Rust handler on the same hardware: tiers 0 to 2 in any language 0.97 to 1.00; C# tier 3 sync on the managed thread per core 0.70 to 0.90 and async 0.50 to 0.80, both unadvertised until the p99-under-allocation-pressure gate is recorded; TypeScript tier 3 sync with one isolate per core 0.50 to 0.80 (the uwebsockets.js entry, the same thread shape with an inline call, reaches 0.92 of ntex-plt on json; the ThreadsafeFunction hop and the request body copy are what sit between the two, and the inline-loop experiment of section 8.5 is the path to close it), async 0.30 to 0.50; Python sync under the GIL 0.15 to 0.30 for the process (one handler thread), async through asyncio 0.05 to 0.15; free-threaded Python scales with handler threads and is unmeasured. The number advertised to TypeScript, Python and C# users is the tier 0 to 2 number, which is the Rust number; the Node facade is scored against uwebsockets.js (2,731,253 json, 711,561 db) rather than bare nodejs and rather than Drogon, that comparison is a harness row that runs before the yardstick is claimed, and tier 2 routes are expected to exceed the uwebsockets.js database numbers because those entries still run postgres.js in JavaScript (extraction, section 2).

## 9. Database drivers

### 9.1 Layout

One I/O driver task per core per endpoint on the core's runtime, owning one socket, one write buffer, one FIFO of in-flight requests with a bounded `max_in_flight`, and one statement cache; handlers on that core enqueue encoded requests and read replies lazily; the driver writes everything queued in one syscall and reads replies in order; a small per-core pool (default 1) covers long transactions and blocking Redis commands; no shared cross-thread pool, because every shared-pool entry in Round 23 was 5 to 20 times slower (carried from research-db-drivers.md section 7 and research-techempower.md 7.3; axum-pg-pool and salvo-pg-pool against 1.3M on db). This is the layout of every top Round 23 database entry, and the top PostgreSQL entries land within about 10 percent of each other whether they use may_postgres, xitca-postgres or a tokio-postgres fork, so the layout matters more than the crate (carried). Drogon's FastDbClient is also one connection per event loop, so the comparison is like for like there; its gap opens on the ORM updates path, which issues one statement per row (drogon 24,034 at q=20 against 58,532 for may-minihttp; extraction).

### 9.2 The resilience gate

TechEmpower issue 8790 (fetched) restarted the database mid-run under the top 20 frameworks and found that only 7 survived gracefully; may-minihttp, just, ntex and others hung, vertx, axum and actix got stuck returning errors, salvo crashed, and the axum configuration that survives "drops its performance to 90K RPS (x6 degradation)" from 550K. Hard requirement on every driver and on the benchmark entry: a per-request sync point (xitca-web-unrealistic's 560,808 updates rests on a single sync point that crashes on database failure and is not a target), reconnect on connection loss, and survival of a database restart mid-run at no more than 5 percent throughput cost, tested in CI with a Docker database that is restarted under load.

### 9.3 Per engine

Wire codecs are in-house no_std crates because postgres-protocol, mysql_common and bson are std-only and drag rand, base64, hmac, sha2, md-5, stringprep, flate2, serde, serde_json, regex, uuid, ahash, indexmap or time into the graph (carried from research-db-drivers.md sections 2.1 and 5); one fuzz harness and one conformance-vector format serve all five engines and all three bindings.

- PostgreSQL (release 2): extended protocol only; one Sync per logical request so an error skips only to its own Sync and results are matched by counting ReadyForQuery; explicit BEGIN, statements and COMMIT pipelined as one unit; binary format code 1 everywhere with in-house decoders for the common OIDs and a text fallback; per-connection LRU statement cache keyed by (SQL, parameter OIDs) with `Close('S')` on eviction, default 256 (judgment); one-round-trip Parse, Bind, Execute, Sync on misses; prepared statements for the benchmark routes at connect time; all statements of a multi-query request written before the first reply is read; single-statement batched updates through `unnest` arrays or pre-generated CASE statements per count (the queries parameter "must be bounded to between 1 and 500", and bulk updates are permitted while "bulk reads are not permissible for selecting"; wiki, fetched); protocol 3.2 negotiation; SCRAM-SHA-256 through `zero-server-crypto` (ASCII passwords first, SASLprep documented as a limitation); COPY and LISTEN/NOTIFY supported but never interleaved with pipelined requests (carried from research-db-drivers.md).
- MySQL and MariaDB (release 3): CLIENT_PROTOCOL_41 and CLIENT_DEPRECATE_EOF, binary result sets for prepared statements, per-connection LRU over COM_STMT_PREPARE ids with COM_STMT_CLOSE on eviction (default 64, judgment), optimistic in-order sends on by default for MariaDB only (MySQL server behavior under back-to-back commands is unverified) plus the MariaDB 0xFFFFFFFF prepare-and-execute path, caching_sha2_password full path only over TLS or a Unix socket, 0xFFFFFF packet continuation, compression off (carried).
- MongoDB (release 3): no wire pipelining; a per-core CMAP-style pool (`maxConnecting` 2, generation invalidation), OP_MSG with payload type 1 for bulk writes, `exhaustAllowed` on getMore, `moreToCome` honored, SCRAM-SHA-256 with speculative authentication in hello; first scope covers standalone and replica-set primary discovery; full SDAM, retryable writes and change streams deferred (carried).
- Redis (release 3): RESP3 through HELLO 3 with RESP2 fallback, per-core pipelined connection flushed after about 200 frames or at the end of the poll cycle, push frames routed to a subscriber channel without consuming reply slots, attributes stripped and attached, dedicated connections for blocking commands; cluster and sentinel later; redis-protocol is the documented fallback because it is the one candidate that builds no_std (carried).
- SQLite (release 3): libsqlite3-sys `bundled` with the sqlite.org hardening options (fetched): `SQLITE_DBCONFIG_DEFENSIVE` on, `SQLITE_MAX_ALLOCATION_SIZE` at or below 100,000,000 (default 2,147,483,391), `SQLITE_PRINTF_PRECISION_LIMIT=100000`, `SQLITE_TRUSTED_SCHEMA=0` and `PRAGMA trusted_schema=OFF`, `sqlite3_hard_heap_limit64`, `sqlite3_limit` on SQL length and expression depth, `sqlite3_progress_handler` against long-running statements; `SQLITE_THREADSAFE=2` with single-owner connections enforced in Rust, `sqlite3_prepare_v3` with `SQLITE_PREPARE_PERSISTENT` behind a per-connection LRU, each connection on a dedicated thread behind an async facade over a bounded channel; an engine-agnostic wrapper trait so a `sqlite-turso` feature can follow once turso reaches 1.0 (carried). This is the one deliberate C library in the data path and `zero-sqlite` is an audited crate for that reason.

### 9.4 Tier 2 executor and the ORM split

The tier 2 executor takes a `QueryPlan` from `zero-sql`, resolves bindings from the request arena, executes on the worker's connection and serializes through the JSON writer or `zero-template` directly into the response buffer. Multi-tenancy is a request-scoped predicate carried in the arena (the Node audit found tenancy as a process global; carried from salvage-map.md 2.2); the audit log is a write path on every driver; migrations and snapshot diff run in Rust with migration files in the host language. The SQL AST whitelists identifiers (`^[A-Za-z_][\w.]*$`) and escapes per dialect, wraps Mongo filter values in `$eq` and rejects `$` keys (the two injection classes from the audit). The class-based `Model`, relations, observers, mutators, seeders, factories and scaffolding stay host-language code over these plan builders (carried from salvage-map.md sections 4 and 6).

## 10. Security model and hardening

### 10.1 Unsafe budget

`[workspace.lints.rust] unsafe_code = "forbid"`, `missing_docs = "deny"`, `unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn = "deny"`, `clippy::mem_forget = "deny"` (the ANSSI rules LANG-UNSAFE "Don't use unsafe blocks", MEM-FORGET "Do not use `mem::forget`" and MEM-FORGET-LINT; checklist fetched). Eight audited crates carry a copied `[lints]` table with only `unsafe_code = "deny"` changed and per-item allows: six in the workspace, `zero-simd` (the dispatch call site and every pointer load and store in the kernels, section 4.3), `zero-server-crypto` (the provider wrapper), `zero-ffi` (the single auditable boundary, as pamoja-ffi states in its lib.rs), `zero-sqlite` (the C library; the binding-first proposal omitted it and the security judge asked for it to be listed), `zero-plugin` (dlopen and the vtable) and `zero-sys` (every raw syscall and socket option, from release 1); and the two Rust binding crates outside the workspace, `bindings/node` (`from_external` where still used for the pooled staging region, ThreadsafeFunction raw pointers, `napi_set_instance_data`) and `bindings/python/packages/native` (PyO3 view classes whose slot is reset per request), which hold the highest-risk unsafe in the product and were outside every lint table in the design before this revision. The binding crates carry the same copied `[lints]` table, are included in the CI lint-table diff and the cargo-geiger inventory, and run Miri on their pure-Rust parts. The CI diff fails if any crate other than these eight gains an `unsafe_code` allow, so `zero-io`, `zero-tls`, `zero-quic`, `zero-rt` and `zero-http` stay at `forbid` by construction. For .NET, `SECURITY.md` enumerates every `unsafe` block, every `[SuppressGCTransition]` site and every `[UnmanagedCallersOnly]` stub in `bindings/dotnet`, and a CODEOWNERS rule requires a named reviewer on any change to those files. Every unsafe block carries a `// SAFETY:` comment enforced by `clippy::undocumented_unsafe_blocks` and `multiple_unsafe_ops_per_block` at deny (LANG-UNSAFE-ENCP "Encapsulation of unsafe features"); manual `Send` and `Sync` implementations only in audited crates with a written justification (LANG-SYNC-TRAITS); a CI script diffs the copied tables against the workspace table because Cargo replaces rather than merges a package lint table; cargo-geiger produces the unsafe inventory for SECURITY.md on each release. The first release therefore carries no in-house reactor and no I/O unsafe outside `zero-sys`: the I/O layer is tokio and mio, which the security judge called the most widely exercised Rust I/O code in existence, and the seam keeps a later completion backend from ever leaking a borrowed slice across an await into the HTTP layer.

### 10.2 Panic policy and release profile

In every no_std crate `clippy::indexing_slicing`, `unwrap_used`, `expect_used`, `panic` and `arithmetic_side_effects` are at deny (LANG-LIMIT-PANIC, LANG-LIMIT-PANIC-SRC, LANG-ARRINDEXING, LANG-ARITH); every malformed input returns `Err`. Release profile: `opt-level = 3`, `lto = "fat"`, `codegen-units = 1`, `overflow-checks = true` (a missed checked operation panics rather than wraps; the cost on the parser hot path is a section 5.7 gate and, if measurable, is relaxed only for `zero-simd` through `[profile.release.package]`), `panic = "unwind"` for every cdylib (the FFI crate must `catch_unwind`; `abort` would take the host process down), `strip = "symbols"`; the standalone binary and the benchmark entry may opt into `panic = "abort"`. Containment does not stop at the FFI exports, because tokio's default `unhandled_panic` behavior is `Ignore`: "Panics on spawned tasks have no impact on the runtime's execution. The panic's error value is forwarded to the task's JoinHandle and all other spawned tasks continue running" (docs.rs Builder, fetched), and the `ShutdownRuntime` alternative "is currently unstable and its implementation is incomplete" (fetched); a panicking connection task whose `JoinHandle` nobody reads would leave the connection half-open and its slot leased forever. So every connection task body runs under `catch_unwind(AssertUnwindSafe(..))`: on a panic the task answers 500 if a head was parsed and nothing was sent, closes the connection, frees and regenerates every slot the connection held, and increments a per-core panic counter that the status callback exposes; the worker's own loop is wrapped the same way and fails closed on a panic outside a task (stop accepting on that core, report `Panic` through the status callback, and in `zero-serve` abort the process, because a core with no worker is a silent outage). A conformance test drives a panicking tier 4 handler and a throwing tier 3 handler in each binding, asserts a 500 for each, and asserts the connection and the core stay usable. Windows control-flow-guard goes into `.cargo/config.toml` target rustflags rather than `RUSTFLAGS` (DENV-CARGO-ENVVARS "Keep default values for compiler environment variables when running cargo" and DENV-CARGO-OPTS "Keep default values for critical variables in cargo profiles"); Linux defaults give PIE, NX, full RELRO and stack probes, verified with `readelf` in CI; a nightly hardened job builds with `-Z stack-protector=all` and `-Z sanitizer=cfi` to keep function-pointer types CFI-clean (carried from research-nostd-and-security.md section 9). Toolchain: a pinned stable release in `rust-toolchain.toml` (DENV-STABLE "Use a stable compilation toolchain"), `Cargo.lock` committed in the workspace and every binding (DENV-CARGO-LOCK).

### 10.3 Verification

Miri with strict provenance and many seeds on the audited and codec crates; ASan and TSan jobs; one libFuzzer target per parser entry point (`zero-http1` request and trailer parsing, `zero-h2`, `zero-hpack`, `zero-h3`, `zero-qpack`, `zero-ws`, `zero-uri`, `zero-qs`, `zero-cookie`, `zero-multipart`, `zero-json`, `zero-jwt`, every wire codec, `zero-sdp`, `zero-stun`, `zero-proto`, the `zero-tls` DER walker and OCSP response parser, `zero-sys` control-message parsing, and the `zero-plugin` ABI validation) with checked-in seed corpora from the RFC examples, the STANDARDS.md vectors and every crash artifact, run as `cargo fuzz run <target> -O -a -s address` with a weekly `-s thread` and `--careful` pass, on Linux only (cargo-fuzz Windows support is contradicted between its README and the Fuzz Book; carried); proptest round-trip laws; a loom model of the slot ownership protocol of section 7.3 and a TSan job that races a late accessor against slot recycle while tier 0 traffic runs on the same core; differential tests against httparse (h1), h2 and hyper (h2), h3 and curl (h3), and the tokio-rs io-uring crate (SQE bytes, if the custom backend is built); every rejection rule is a fuzz dictionary entry.

### 10.4 Limits (all configurable; starting values)

HTTP/1.1: request line 8,192 octets; header field 8,192; 100 headers (parser table 64 by default); 32 KiB head; header read timeout 30 s; idle keep-alive 60 s; body read idle 60 s; request total 300 s; body 1 MiB unless a route opts in; 1,000 requests per connection; 8 pipelined requests in flight by default with a codec cap of 32; chunk sizes as checked u64 hex with a 16-digit cap; chunk extensions 256 octets; trailers 4 KiB in a separate table with the allow list of section 6.2; receive buffer blocks 8 KiB, leased on readiness; a global connection semaphore; a per-core request-memory budget (leased receive buffers plus buffered bodies plus leased response buffers; 256 MiB per core by default, judgment) past which the core pauses accepts, so 16,384 connections each buffering a 1 MiB body cannot commit 16 GiB; a per-core bound of 16 queued tier 3 batches past which new tier 3 requests get 503 with `Retry-After`; a lease timeout equal to the request total timeout. TLS: handshake timeout 10 s; 1,024 in-progress handshakes per core. HTTP/2: 100 concurrent streams, 16,384 frame size, 32,768 header list, 4,096 table, the h2 crate reset limits plus a 200-per-10-s reset window. HTTP/3 and QUIC: 100 bidirectional and 3 unidirectional streams plus a reserved allowance, 1 MiB connection data, 256 KiB per stream, 30 s idle, 1,350-byte receive payload, `SETTINGS_MAX_FIELD_SECTION_SIZE` 32,768, QPACK capacity 0 and blocked streams 0, QPACK integer cap 2^30, a RESET_STREAM and STOP_SENDING window closing with H3_EXCESSIVE_LOAD. WebSocket: 16 MiB message cap, fragment and control-frame budgets. gRPC 4 MiB messages, SDP 64 KiB, session cookies 4,096 bytes (the Node defaults). All live in `zero-limits`; the HTTP/1.1 values are carried from research-nostd-and-security.md section 7 except the two fetched here (the 8,000-octet request-line recommendation and the reject-and-close rule for conflicting framing).

### 10.5 Smuggling, hash flooding, secrets

Ambiguous framing is 400 plus close in both roles (standalone and behind a proxy); Transfer-Encoding obfuscation is an unknown coding and is 501 plus close, following the RFC 9112 section 6.1 SHOULD (fetched; section 6.2 lists the full rule set). Attacker-keyed fields (headers, query, cookies, multipart parts) are bounded `Vec<(Name, Value)>` with linear scan, never a hash map with hashbrown's default hasher (carried from research-nostd-and-security.md 12.4). Every MAC, token, session id, CSRF token and JWT signature is compared through `zero-server-crypto::verify_mac` and `verify_token` over aws-lc-rs `constant_time::verify_slices_are_equal` (2026-10-01: subtle 2.6.1 last released 2024-06-24, outside the adoption window, and aws-lc-rs is already a direct dependency; a ring build would use subtle, which rustls pulls in anyway, because ring 0.17.14 keeps its constant-time compare deprecated and hidden); secret newtypes never implement `PartialEq` (grep-tested); secrets live in `zeroize::Zeroizing<Box<[u8]>>` (2026-10-01: a boxed slice cannot reallocate, so no copy is left behind; `SecretBytes`) ("a wrapper for any Z: Zeroize type which implements a Drop handler which zeroizes dropped values", docs.rs zeroize 1.9.0, fetched) allocated once at final size, wrapped in an in-house `Secret<T>` newtype in `zero-server-crypto` with no `Debug` output and no `PartialEq`; the `secrecy` crate is not used, because zeroize is already on the allowlist through rustls and a second crate for the same job would need its own row.

### 10.6 Runtime posture

The shipped release 1 graph contains no io_uring path (section 5.3). When `io-compio` or a custom backend ships, the operator documentation carries a note that Docker's default seccomp profile blocks `io_uring_setup`, `io_uring_enter` and `io_uring_register` "due to security vulnerabilities that can be exploited to break out of containers" (fetched) and that the moby PR that removed them cites Google disabling io_uring on ChromeOS, Android and its production servers (fetched); the `--io=epoll` switch is documented; the epoll path is tested with the same weight as any completion backend. The Google kCTF io_uring statistics that the research files quote were not fetchable by the judges or in this task and are treated as unverified. kTLS is opt-in with the fallback exercised in CI; 0-RTT is off; server push is rejected on every protocol; every binding runs on the system allocator; the core installs no signal handlers and no global allocator inside a host process.

### 10.7 Supply chain and provenance

cargo-deny with the populated allowlist of section 11; cargo-vet beside it with the mozilla, google, bytecode-alliance, isrg, embark-studios and zcash audit sets imported, exemptions only with a named owner and a review date, trust entries only for the rustls organization with an expiration (LIBS-VETTING-DIRECT "Validation of Direct Third-Party Dependencies" and LIBS-VETTING-TRANSITIVE); a weekly job running `cargo audit bin` over released binaries, `cargo outdated` and `cargo geiger` (LIBS-AUDIT, LIBS-OUTDATED); every shipped cdylib built with `cargo auditable`; a CycloneDX SBOM and `actions/attest` on every binary, wheel, nupkg and npm tarball through reusable workflows (SLSA Build L3); CodeQL for actions, csharp, javascript-typescript, python and rust with pamoja's `paths-ignore` for the napi glue; reproducible builds with an exact toolchain pin, Docker images by digest, `--remap-path-prefix` and `CFLAGS=-ffile-prefix-map`, `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` from the commit, and a CI job that builds the release cdylib twice in separate containers and fails on a SHA-256 mismatch (carried from research-tls-and-deps.md sections 6.2 to 6.5 and research-nostd-and-security.md section 10).

### 10.8 Plugin trust model

A tier 4 dynamic plugin is unsandboxed native code with the full privilege of the process. `zero-plugin` loads only cdylibs named in operator configuration with an expected SHA-256 per file, never a path derived from request input. It opens the file once and both hashes and loads from that one descriptor, so there is no window between the check and the load in which the file on disk can be swapped: on Linux the bytes are copied into a `memfd_create` descriptor, hashed there, and loaded with `dlopen` of `/proc/self/fd/N`; on Windows the handle is opened with exclusive share mode, hashed, and passed to `LoadLibrary` while still held (the descriptor and handle calls live in `zero-sys`). It refuses a plugin directory that is world-writable or not owned by the process owner, checks `zero_plugin_abi_version` before calling `zero_plugin_register`, resolves only the documented symbols, and is off by default in every binding (a host application enables it explicitly). A conformance vector swaps the file between the hash and the load and asserts refusal. A plugin that panics is caught at the vtable boundary and the plugin is disabled for the process lifetime. Signature verification (Ed25519 over the file hash through `zero-server-crypto`) is an option, not a default. This model is a precondition for the crate to ship, as the security judge asked.

### 10.9 Regression catalog

The roughly 120 defects of the 2026-09-27 audit become failing-first tests in the crate that owns the behavior (identifier injection, Mongo operator injection, urlencoded prototype pollution and array caps, decompression bombs with output caps, dotfile segments, percent-decoding errors, JWT algorithm confusion, JWKS kid and alg matching, WebAuthn userVerified, TURN loops and RFC 1918 relays, protobuf 64-bit varints and presence, gRPC deadlines, WebSocket framing, fetch double write, tenancy isolation under concurrency, bounded maps with expiry), kept in a gitignored `conformance/regressions.md` until fixed (carried from salvage-map.md section 2.2).

## 11. Dependency policy and the allowlist

Two tiers (carried from research-tls-and-deps.md section 6): zero third-party crates in every crate that neither terminates TLS, hosts the QUIC transport, sits on the runtime seam, makes raw operating-system calls, wraps the C library nor crosses a language boundary (every no_std crate, plus `zero-rt`, `zero-http`, `zero-static`, `zero-policy`, `zero-realtime`, `zero-cache`, `zero-db` and the drivers other than SQLite, `zero-orm`, `zero-auth`, `zero-compress`, `zero-grpc`, `zero-observe`, `zero-webrtc`, `zero-fetch`); a pinned allowlist elsewhere (`zero-io`, `zero-sys`, `zero-tls`, `zero-server-crypto`, `zero-quic`, `zero-sqlite`, `zero-ffi`, the bindings). Enforcement rests on the cargo-deny semantics fetched in this task: "If the `allow` list has one or more entries, then any crate not in that list will be denied", `multiple-versions = "deny"`, `wildcards = "deny"`, `external-default-features = "deny"` (the lint "for when the `default` feature is enabled on a crate not in the workspace"), `build.allow-build-scripts` enumerated (when omitted "all crates are allowed to have a build script"), `build.executables = "deny"`, `[sources] unknown-registry` and `unknown-git` denied, `[advisories] yanked = "deny"` with every ignore carrying a reason and a review date, `[graph] exclude-dev = true`, licenses as pamoja (MIT, Apache-2.0, Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception, BSD-2-Clause, BSD-3-Clause, ISC, Unicode-3.0, Zlib; the MPL-2.0 exception for cbindgen only; a CDLA-Permissive-2.0 exception for webpki-roots only, with the rationale in `deny.toml` that it is Mozilla's root store data, not code). An explicit `deny` list names bindgen, libclang-sys and clang-sys, so a target outside the pregenerated-binding matrix below fails `cargo deny` rather than silently pulling a C++ toolchain into the build. `cargo deny check` runs once per manifest (workspace, `bindings/node`, `bindings/python/packages/native`).

Binary matrix. aws-lc-sys ships pregenerated bindings for eleven targets (aarch64-apple-darwin, aarch64-pc-windows-msvc, aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu, aarch64-unknown-linux-musl, i686-pc-windows-msvc, i686-unknown-linux-gnu, x86_64-apple-darwin, x86_64-pc-windows-gnu, x86_64-pc-windows-msvc, x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, x86_64-unknown-linux-musl) and requires bindgen and libclang elsewhere, and NASM on Windows x86 and x86-64 unless `prebuilt-nasm` (aws-lc-sys README, fetched by the security review; not re-fetched here). The published prebuilt matrix for npm, PyPI and NuGet is therefore pinned to seven of those targets (linux gnu and musl on x64 and arm64, darwin x64 and arm64, windows x64 msvc) and stated in each release workflow; armv7, riscv64, FreeBSD and any later target are source builds with the aws-lc-rs provider or prebuilt on ring, never a bindgen build. `prebuilt-nasm` is not enabled: it ships prebuilt object files inside the crate, which is a supply-chain decision the design declines, so the Windows release runner installs NASM by pinned version and the choice is recorded in `deny.toml` with that rationale.

| Python binding only | pyo3 0.29 with `abi3-py310`, pyo3-ffi, pyo3-build-config, pyo3-macros and the measured 13-crate graph; pyo3-async-runtimes only if section 18 decides for it | pyo3-stub-gen dev-only; the crate is audited (section 10.1) |
| .NET and C | cbindgen 0.29, build-only in `zero-ffi` | MPL-2.0 exception as in pamoja |
| Dev-only (excluded by `exclude-dev`) | httparse (in `fuzz/` only, under the owner's currency exception of 2026-10-02), h2, hyper, h3, h3-quinn, tokio-rustls, io-uring, compio-driver adapters in `zero-bench`, rcgen, proptest, libfuzzer-sys, arbitrary, criterion, tokio-postgres, redis, mongodb | oracles, interoperability peers and benches; never shipped |

Explicitly off the list, with the reason: tokio-rustls (TLS is driven over the seam), serde and serde_json (the writer and codecs are in house; bindings convert host values to the builder API), http, hyper and h2 at runtime, log and tracing outside the `http3` feature (the core has its own observability surface), x509-parser and der (an in-house DER walker for AIA, serial and OCSP), ktls (in house), brotli and zlib-rs (compression code is attack surface; the in-house DEFLATE and gzip encoders replace them and brotli stays an open question), core_affinity (`zero-sys` wrappers over libc and windows-sys instead), redis-protocol (fallback only), postgres-protocol, mysql_common, bson, fred, rusqlite, turso (in house or deferred), secrecy (zeroize does the job), simdutf8 (in house), aya and libbpf-rs (the opt-in steering loader is raw `bpf(2)` in `zero-sys`), bindgen and libclang (denied outright), and any crate with a build script not enumerated above.

## 12. Conformance and testing

### 12.1 The standards registry

`docs/STANDARDS.md` (148 verified sources, 515 conformance statements written "to become test names"; carried from salvage-map.md section 2.1) migrates into `docs/standards.toml` in pamoja's shape (`[[group]]` and entries with `key`, `chapter`, `designation`, `body`, `subject`, `url`, `evidence`, `at`, `anchor` in {vector, rule, interop, internal}), with the `Module path` column rewritten from `lib/...` to crate paths, the `node:sqlite` row replaced by a row against the sqlite.org documentation fetched here, and rows added for RFC 9000, 9001, 9002, 9114, 9204, 7838 and 8470. Each statement becomes one `#[test]` or one vector whose name is the statement and whose doc comment cites the section. Every row carries a `release` field (1, 2 or 3) naming the release that ships the feature it covers; `xtask standards --check` fails only when a row at or below the current release has no test and reports the later rows as pending, so migrating all 515 statements in release 1 does not leave CI red until parity. `xtask links` checks every URL. Rows added in this revision: RFC 9112 sections 2.2, 3.2.2, 6.1 (501) and 6.3, RFC 9110 sections 5.5, 6.5.1 and 8.6 (section 6.2), the six RFC 6960 section 3.2 acceptance requirements (section 6.7), the mTLS revocation options, and the `responseSplitting` vectors (section 6.3). The "Citations to re-check by hand" list becomes the first backlog of the driver crates.

### 12.2 Conformance vectors

`conformance/vectors.json` in pamoja's format (one committed file generated by `cargo run -p zero-examples --example conformance_vectors`, sorted keys, hex for bytes, a `tolerance` field), CI regenerates it and fails on a diff, and all three bindings assert it (`bindings/node/conformance.js`, `bindings/python/tests/test_conformance.py`, the .NET smoke project). Sections from release 1: `http1Parser` (request bytes in, head ranges or rejection out), `router`, `jwt`, `cookies`, `rateLimit`, `qpack`, `h3Frames`; later `hpack`, `h2Frames`, `ws`, `sse`, `pgProto`, `mysqlProto`, `bson`, `resp`, `sdp`, `stun`, `proto`. Published vectors from the RFCs are preferred where they exist (RFC 7541 Appendix C, RFC 9204 Appendix B).

### 12.3 The vitest corpus and the API surface

The corpus was classified in this revision by API surface rather than by suite name (a script over `test/**/*.test.js` counting `it(` and `test(` cases and flagging every file that uses Node's http object API: `res.setHeader`, `res.statusCode`, `res.writeHead`, `res.write`, `res.end`, `res.getHeader`, `req.on`, `req.headers`, `req.url`, `req.method`, `req.socket`, `req.pipe`, `app.handler`, `http.createServer`): 128 files and 7,684 cases in all; 40 files with 2,970 cases use those Node http objects directly and 88 files with 4,714 cases do not. Within the ten suites that assert observable HTTP behavior (app, http, middleware, body, auth, realtime, grpc, observe, errors, env: 3,383 cases), 2,659 cases sit in files that use the Node http objects (all of http, middleware and body, most of grpc, auth, errors and observe) and 724 run through the facade API alone (`doFetch` against an app); the remaining 4,301 cases are ORM (2,319), adapter (861), WebRTC (528), docs (532, of which 242 also touch the Node objects) and package suites, which are implementation-detail or host-language tests. The salvage claim is therefore split. The 724 facade-only cases run in release 1 through a `test/_shim/` module map plus a scripted rewrite of relative `require` paths, since vitest's alias option does not redirect CommonJS `require` calls. The 2,659 cases that address `IncomingMessage` and `ServerResponse` need a Node-compatible request and response emulation (`Readable` and `Writable` over the slot accessors, `writeHead`, `setHeader`, `getHeader`, `on('data')`, `end`), which is its own line in section 16 (15 to 25 days, judgment), carries a per-property boundary cost the facade's own API does not, and ships in release 3 with the suites it exercises (auth, body, grpc and observe cannot run before their features exist), so it is not part of the release 1 Node binding line. The earlier figure of "3,400 cases through a 5 to 8 day shim" is withdrawn. Implementation-detail suites (adapter internals, fake timers on internal keep-alives, the 21 coverage-only files) are dropped; `test/_helpers.js` (`doFetch`, `waitFor`) transfers unchanged; the documentation example runner (`test/docs/manifest-validation.test.js`) transfers with the docs data format (carried from salvage-map.md section 2.3). `conformance/api-surface.json` is the contract every binding's generated declarations are diffed against (section 8.7).

### 12.4 CI matrix

fmt and clippy in the official `rust:latest` Docker image (the local scoop toolchain has neither; the pamoja's local rules file recipe), workspace tests on both `io-tokio` and `io-compio`, the no_std host build with `--no-default-features` and the bare-metal cross-compile, an MSRV job, `cargo deny check` per manifest, `cargo vet`, the fuzz smoke job, Miri on the audited and codec crates, ASan and TSan, the reproducibility double build, the conformance regeneration diff, `xtask docs --check`, `xtask standards --check`, `xtask version --check`, `xtask release --plan`, the three binding pipelines (build, generated-contract diff, smoke, conformance, guides), CodeQL, and the resilience test that restarts the database container under load.

### 12.5 The benchmark harness and the reference host

The FrameworkBenchmarks repository is archived (GitHub API, fetched: `archived: true`, `pushed_at` 2026-03-24), and its results site returns no data to a fetch (carried), so no official round will certify a result. The acceptance measurement is a self-run of the archived toolset at commit 523534bb with the unmodified Round 23 Drogon entry (Drogon commit 96919df4, `threads_num 0`, `is_fast true`, `connection_number 1`, SyncPlugin; both commits carried from research-techempower.md, not re-fetched) beside the two `zero-bench` entries. The owner's documented environment is one Windows 11 desktop, so the acceptance is tiered and each row of section 13 states the tier it is judged on: tier A, json, db, query, fortunes and updates on one rented Linux host (or two bare-metal instances on the same switch) where the link is not the limiter, reported as a ratio against the pinned Drogon entry on the same hardware; tier B, plaintext reported only as a ratio against the ceiling reference entry on whatever link exists, since a 10 GbE or slower link caps every entry at the same number; tier C, a final run on rented bare metal with a 25 or 40 GbE link between load generator and server plus a database host, comparable to Round 23's ConnectX-6 40 Gbps link (fetched), which is the only tier on which a plaintext ratio against Drogon is published. Hardware rental and setup is a line in section 16. Rules: the `zero-server` entry goes through the router with the `zero-limits` defaults (owner decision 2026-10-02; the earlier text added `zero-policy`) and satisfies the wiki's requirements (a real HTTP implementation, `Server` and `Date` headers, `Content-Length` or `Transfer-Encoding`, no gzip, disk logging off, pipelining at 256 to 16,384 connections, queries bounded to 1 to 500, no bulk reads; fetched) so it is classified Realistic and is the product number compared with Drogon; the `zero-server-plt` entry is the raw h1 handler with no router, declared with approach Stripped and classification Platform exactly as ntex declares its `plt` entries (frameworks/Rust/ntex/benchmark_config.json, fetched: `plt`, `plt-neon` and `plt-neon-uring` are "Stripped" and "Platform"; `default` and `db` are "Realistic" and "Micro"), and is compared with the ceiling reference only; the Drogon container passes every verification before its numbers are used (every actix entry failed to start in Round 23 with "ERROR: Problem starting actix-*" in the status fields of the extraction, and Drogon failed in Round 22; carried); five interleaved runs; medians compared; a win required in every run; ratios published beside absolute numbers; error counters at zero at every level. The reference host: a ceiling reference entry from the archived tree (libreactor or faf, both 28.0M at zero errors in Round 23) runs in the same session to establish the link ceiling of the self-run hardware, so that a plaintext ratio is reported against both Drogon and the ceiling; `nodejs` and `uwebsockets.js` from the same tree run as the Node yardsticks; current Drogon is measured separately from the pinned entry. Within-run noise for identical code is 0.06 to 1.9 percent; run-to-run variance is unverified, which is why five interleaved runs and a win in every run are required (carried from research-techempower.md section 3.11).

The same harness records the section 5.7 gates (bytes per idle connection with lazy leasing, cgroup CPU per request, the 16-connection escape, the 16,384-connection level, the libuv wake CPU cost, .NET p99 under allocation pressure, mimalloc inside the three hosts, overflow checks), the per-binding boundary budgets of section 8.6 cell by cell, the Node json handler row against uwebsockets.js, the Python GIL contention row, the fortunes levers one at a time (section 13), and the resilience gate of section 9.2. Before release 1 planning is frozen, `bench-probe.js`, `bench-probe-inflight.js`, `bench_probe.py` and `pinvoke-bench` are rerun inside `node:24`, `python:3.13` and `mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk` Linux containers and the section 8.6 budgets are restated from those numbers.

Release 1 (owner decision 2026-10-02, which replaces the tiers above for release 1): the benchmark runs in Docker on the owner's Ryzen 9 9950X3D desktop under WSL2, the server and the load generator on separate cpusets and the fuzz container paused, by the method of `RULES.md` (Conventions): the median of five interleaved runs, the ratio against each entry measured in the same session beside every absolute number, every error counter at zero, and the raw data with the command that reproduces it committed under `bench/results/<date>/`. The rented tier A and tier C runs are waived for release 1, no ratio gates the release, and the ratios are published as measured with the hardware stated as one desktop under WSL2. The Realistic entry is the one that goes through the router with the `zero-limits` defaults. The owner's go decision is this decision, dated 2026-10-02 (roadmap R.2).

## 13. Performance targets per test, with the Drogon baseline and margin

All reference values are Round 23 numbers on the Round 23 hardware (Xeon Gold 6330, 56 cores, 64 GB, 40 Gbps; fetched) from the extraction run in this task; the self-run publishes ratios on its own hardware. "Expected" is judgment anchored to Realistic entries on the shipped runtime shape (one tokio current-thread runtime per core: hyper, xitca-web, ntex, axum, and their `-db` and `-pg` entries) with the Stripped and stackful entries named only as ceilings; nothing here is a measurement of a built system. The reference for each row is the Realistic tokio precedent, not the best Rust entry, because the design before this revision anchored plaintext and json on ntex-plt, which is a Stripped Platform entry (benchmark_config.json, fetched), while requiring the product entry to be Realistic. Minimum win is a ratio over Drogon with zero errors at every level unless the row says otherwise, and each row names the acceptance tier of section 12.5 it is judged on. Release 1 is judged against none of these rows: the rented tiers are waived for it and its ratios are published as measured on the owner's desktop (section 12.5, owner decision 2026-10-02), so the rows stay targets in the plan.

Cross-cutting: the kernel I/O backend changes none of these by more than the ntex tokio-against-compio spread (plaintext 7 percent, json 2 percent, db 3 percent, fortunes 5.5 percent, updates 1 percent; extraction), which is why the numbers are published on `io-tokio` and the epoll fallback, and why fortunes, where 5.5 percent is the whole distance between 1.05 and 1.10, is the one row with a backend-specific deliverable; `overflow-checks = true`, `panic = "unwind"` and full error handling may cost a few percent that the Round 23 leaders do not pay (may-minihttp ships with overflow checks off and panic abort; carried), which the harness quantifies; plaintext and json are client- and link-bound, so a weaker load generator shrinks every gap and the ceiling reference entry is what makes the self-run interpretable. The hardware-efficiency numbers (CPU per request, bytes per idle connection) are gates, not targets, because no source publishes a value to beat.

`crates/<product>-ffi/build.rs` and `cbindgen.toml` (header regenerated on every build inside the checkout, written only on change, CI diff-checked), the FFI lib.rs conventions (`#![allow(unsafe_code)]` as the single auditable boundary, the `#[repr(C)]` status enum with `Ok = 0`, thread-local `LAST_ERROR`, opaque handles with `*_free`, panics caught and reported as `Panic`); `bindings/python/pytest.ini`, `tests/test_guides.py`, `packages/native/src/stub_gen.rs`, `raw.py`, the hatchling per-package layout with a PEP 420 namespace and `py.typed`; `bindings/dotnet/src/*.Native/{NativeHandle,Status,*Exception,OwnedString,OwnedBuffer}.cs`, `Directory.Build.props` (net8.0, `AllowUnsafeBlocks`, `TreatWarningsAsErrors`), the smoke and guides projects, `docfx.json`; `web/serve.mjs`; `deny.toml` with an empty ignore list and the cbindgen exception; the Docker-run rustfmt and clippy recipe in the local rules file; the `justfile` recipes (fmt, lint, nostd, test, deny, docs-check, version-check, release-plan, release, ci) minus the dashboard and broker recipes; Conventions kept: rustdoc with `# Arguments`, `# Returns` and `# Errors` sections on every public item, `missing_docs = "deny"`, crate READMEs generated from lib.rs and CI-checked, tests anchored to the specification's own vectors, parsers of untrusted input carrying proptest tests, examples and guides that build values with library calls rather than pasting byte blobs, README claims audited in the same change that ships or removes a feature, planning markdown under a gitignored directory, commits authored as molexxxx with no AI attribution.

Not depended upon: the pamoja crates themselves. `pamoja-core`'s error shape and `pamoja-codec`'s six-line `Codec<T>` trait are copied into `zero-core` rather than depended upon, so the server's release cadence and error type do not couple to pamoja; `pamoja-session` is the one crate cheap to share if a lightweight secured channel outside TLS is ever needed, and the rest (security, audit, telemetry) are device-shaped and stay in pamoja.

## 15. What zero-server salvages, and how the npm package transitions

### 15.1 Salvaged, by destination

- `docs/STANDARDS.md` into `docs/standards.toml` as the conformance registry and test-name generator (section 12.1); estimated 3 to 5 engineer-days saved (carried from salvage-map.md).
- The 2026-09-27 audit's roughly 120 findings as the regression catalog (section 10.9); about 10 days saved.
- About 724 facade-only vitest cases through the `test/_shim/` map in release 1 (about 20 days of test writing saved against 3 to 5 days for the shim), and about 2,659 further cases through the Node-compatible request and response emulation in release 3 (about 80 days saved against 15 to 25 days for the emulation), classified by API surface in section 12.3.
- The JSDoc surface (238 exports, 2,859 `@param`, 1,112 `@returns`, 484 `@example`) as `conformance/api-surface.json` and the seed of the guides in three languages (section 8.7); 8 to 12 days saved. The hand-written `types/*.d.ts` (20 files, 12 compile errors) are not the contract and are dropped.
- Router semantics and tests, the error registry and status mapping, JWT verification and claim rules, the ORM's model and query description layer as tier 2 plan builders, the docs data format and its example runner, the scope manifest idea as `docs/capabilities.toml`, the TLS option names, the limit constants already chosen in the Node code.
- The measured Node baselines (71 to 72 percent of bare `node:http` with debug logging on; the 10.9 microsecond router miss; uWebSockets.js at 2.4 to 3.2 times `node:http` non-pipelined and about 14 times pipelined in a pinned Linux container) as the numbers the Node facade must beat (carried from salvage-map.md section 2.7).

### 15.2 Dropped

The in-house Node wire-protocol driver plan, the TypeScript conversion of `lib/`, the `packages/` generator and its 14 runtime stubs, hand-written types, `lib/cluster.js` as a feature (kept as a shim), the memory, event-loop and disk checks, default-on debug logging, HTTP/2 server push, the WebRTC media adapters (mediasoup, LiveKit, ffmpeg MCU, recording, ingress, cascade), the E2EE helpers, the JSON file ORM adapter, `PluginManager`, `DatabaseView` and `Query.cache()` until a core design exists, the live Node playground, and the badge and stub publishing scripts (carried from salvage-map.md section 4).

### 15.3 The npm transition

- 1.1.1 (security patch, no API change): the audit's critical and high fixes already in the working tree plus the remaining ones listed in salvage-map.md section 3, the NPM_TOKEN renewal and the release-on-bump fix (v1.0.1 and v1.1.0 went out by manual dispatch under the `alpha` dist-tag).
- 1.2.0 (correctness and types): transactions, audit and tenancy on every adapter, the Model and CLI fixes, the HTTP and gRPC correctness list, `types/index.d.ts` compiling with `skipLibCheck=false`, and removal of the "documented but not implemented" claims from the docs.
- After 1.2.0 the Node repository takes security patches only.
- 2.0.0: `@zero-server/sdk` becomes the TypeScript facade over `@zero-server/native` with `@zero-server/core` and one scoped facade per capability (the pamoja three-tier shape), exact-pinned; the existing package name, the `createApp` surface, the error classes, the Model classes, `clusterize` as a shim and the `env` loader keep their shapes; the vitest subset is the acceptance suite; anything in the salvage map's drop list is a documented breaking change in the 2.0.0 CHANGELOG.

### 15.4 Parity gate

Release 3 is "at parity" when every export in `conformance/api-surface.json` minus the section 15.2 drop list exists in all three contract tiers, every `docs/standards.toml` row has a test or vector, the vitest subset passes against the Node facade, the regression catalog is empty, the resilience gate passes on every driver, the release 1 harness targets still hold on the parity build, and the molexcloud-remake application runs on the Node facade with none of its sixteen workarounds (roadmap R.8).

## 16. Effort (judgment)

Engineer-days for one senior Rust engineer with the pamoja scaffolding copied and the research files as the specification; every figure is judgment, not sourced. The release 1 figure takes the pragmatic proposal's 74-day plan, adds the grafts the judges priced (`zero-rt` as its own crate, the binding-first `zero-ffi` plus Node line, `zero-limits` and the `zero-policy` subset, the `io-compio` backend, the generated header plus smoke tests, `api-surface.json` diffing, the gate harnesses, the `zero-h3` and `zero-qpack` codecs), and then adds the work the feasibility review found the same document makes mandatory but did not price: the second TLS driver, `zero-sys`, the slot ownership protocol, the WebSocket and SSE ABI, the Node isolate pool, the CI build matrix, the hardware for the acceptance run, and the Linux probe rerun. The vitest shim moves out of the Node line to the release that ships the suites it exercises.

A calendar quarter holds about 63 working days, so release 1 needs two engineers for more than a quarter or three for one: one on the runtime, `zero-sys` and the HTTP crates, one on `zero-rt`, `zero-ffi` and the Node binding, and the harness and CI matrix shared; the critical path with two engineers is about 110 days (judgment).

Parity with zero-server 1.1.0 on top of release 1 (the pragmatic proposal's parity table with the binding-first FFI lines and the additions of this revision): HTTP/2 in house 22; `zero-hpack` sharing 4; streaming request and response bodies on the handler ABI in all three bindings 8; `zero-quic`, the h3 adapter, Alt-Svc with the operator gate, the CID handoff path, the interop runner 18, plus the opt-in eBPF steering program with its `bpf(2)` loader in `zero-sys` and its privileged-runner test 5, plus the headless-browser h3 check 2; body parsers 8; remaining policy and middleware 12; DEFLATE and gzip in house 12 (brotli undecided, not counted); sessions and trusted devices 6; `zero-server-crypto` remainder 6; auth stack including the trust store requirement and the `zero-fetch` egress policy 30; database codecs and drivers 200 (range 170 to 230), with the fortunes levers measured one at a time; `zero-sql` and `zero-orm` 30; gRPC and protobuf 28; observability 12; WebRTC signaling, STUN, TURN 24; `zero-fetch` 10; Python binding facade with the handler thread pool, the GIL contention benchmark, and wheels including free-threaded 22; .NET binding facade with the managed thread per core, the p99 gate, and NuGet 22; the Node inline-loop experiment 6; `zero-serve` CLI and typed env 6; kTLS, OCSP with full verification and its fuzz target, mTLS with CRLs 11; the Node-compatible request and response emulation for the 2,659 vitest cases that need it 20 (range 15 to 25); conformance migration remainder (standards.toml rows, regression catalog) 12; documentation site and guides in three languages 12. Parity total about 550 on top of release 1, about 750 cumulative (range 640 to 880). The database line dominates and parallelizes cleanly with a second engineer. A custom io_uring backend is not required for parity and is not counted.

## 17. Risks

1. updates q=1 has no margin: every Realistic Rust entry lands at 1.01 to 1.05 times Drogon (extraction), so the published deliverable is parity plus the q=20 ratio, and 1.10 is a stretch that needs something no leader does under the resilience gate.
2. fortunes has no Realistic precedent at 1.10 on the shipped runtime shape (ntex-db 1.088 with a buffer-direct template already), so the `io-tokio` deliverable is 1.05 and the 1.10 target rests on the `io-compio` io_uring path (ntex-db-compio 1.148) and on levers (allocation-free row decode, borrowed-slice sort, one writev) that are unmeasured until the harness runs them one at a time.
3. plaintext at 256 connections has no Realistic tokio entry above 1.06 times Drogon and the 16,384-connection level has none above 16.0M; the 1.10 deliverables at the best level and at 16,384 rest on hyper and xitca-web (1.19 to 1.37), and every figure above 18.4M at the best level or 16.0M at 16,384 is a stretch with no tokio precedent outside Stripped entries. The Platform entry exists so a raw-handler number can be published honestly beside the ceiling reference without labeling it Realistic.
4. No official round will certify the result; hardware differs; run-to-run variance is unverified; plaintext and json are link- and client-bound, so the ceiling reference entry and five interleaved runs are what make the ratio meaningful.
5. `overflow-checks = true`, `panic = "unwind"` and full error handling may cost a few percent the leaders do not pay; unmeasured until the harness runs.
6. In-house HTTP/2 and HTTP/1.1 replace fuzzed, widely deployed crates; the oracles (httparse, h2, hyper), the RFC vectors, the section 10.5 budgets, the fuzz targets and the `h2-crate` bring-up feature are the compensating controls.
7. compio-driver is pre-1.0 (max stable 0.12.5, 0.13.0-beta.1 one day old at the time of writing; fetched) and single-organization; the seam limits but does not remove the cost of an API break, which is why it ships only as a non-default backend until section 5.3's conditions hold.
8. io_uring is blocked by default Docker seccomp (fetched), so most containers run epoll; the CPU and memory claims for completion I/O rest on documented mechanisms and one non-HTTP benchmark (monoio, fetched), not on HTTP measurements, which is why they are gates.
9. The Windows cost of the mio path is contradicted between two mio documents (fetched) and is unverified until measured; Windows accept is structurally different (one listener, handoff) and Windows QUIC steering is unverified.
10. Node tier 3 with one isolate per core matches the uwebsockets.js thread shape but keeps a ThreadsafeFunction hop whose CPU cost is unmeasured (only wall time was measured, 1 to 2 microseconds per request at the json test's 9 in flight per core); the inline-loop experiment is the fallback if that hop costs the yardstick. Python under the GIL runs one handler thread for the process, the contended cost is unmeasured, and free-threaded scaling is unmeasured and needs version-specific wheels (pyo3.rs, fetched). All binding measurements are Windows desktop numbers whose ThreadsafeFunction rows are libuv wake latencies; Citrine is Linux on 56 logical CPUs; the Linux container rerun is a release 1 line and the budgets are provisional until it runs.
11. The bounded dispatcher and the in-flight count per target are load-bearing: at one batch in flight, 8 items per crossing cost 2,218 ns per item and 16 cost 1,170 ns, against 187 and 114 ns with 8 batches in flight (rerun-node-probe-inflight.txt); the 503 back-pressure path past 16 queued batches per core is untested under a real load generator.
18. The slot ownership protocol adds one atomic compare-and-swap per accessor call on the tier 3 path and an epoch acknowledgment per batch; the cost is unmeasured and is part of the section 8.6 micro-harness, and a wrong state transition is a cross-tenant data exposure, which is why the loom model and the TSan race test are release 1 work rather than hardening.
19. Release 1 tier 3 handlers are buffered only; a user who needs uploads above the body limit, proxy routes or long streamed responses from host code waits for release 2, and the 1.1.0 Node package keeps those users until then.
20. The tiered acceptance depends on rented hardware; without the tier C run there is no plaintext ratio against Drogon, only ratios against the ceiling reference, and the design says so rather than publishing a tier B number as a Drogon comparison. For release 1 the owner waived the rented tiers (2026-10-02, section 12.5): the ratios measured on one desktop under WSL2 are published as measured, with that hardware stated, and none is presented as a tier A or tier C result.
12. MongoDB is the largest and least certain driver scope; MySQL optimistic sends are unverified against MySQL server; bundled SQLite is C; in-house SCRAM, caching_sha2 and SASLprep are security-sensitive and need vectors.
13. quinn-proto brings `tracing` and a dozen crates into the `http3` feature; aws-lc-sys brings 67 MB of C source and NASM on Windows; ring calls itself an experiment; rustls 0.24 re-cuts the allowlist and every binding lockfile together; two providers in one build split getrandom and trip `multiple-versions = "deny"`.
14. HTTP/3 doubles the transport surface on a UDP path that firewalls and container port mappings treat differently; Alt-Svc advertised while UDP is unreachable delays clients, so the self-probe and `Alt-Svc: clear` are mandatory.
15. The local toolchain cannot run rustfmt or clippy; skipping the Docker step breaks CI, and a crate already on crates.io cannot be republished at the same version. NuGet trusted-publishing policies and PyPI project names must exist before the first tag; the unprobed `zero-<capability>` names may collide.
16. The plugin loader is unsandboxed native code inside a host process; it ships only with the section 10.8 trust model and off by default.
17. Every effort figure is judgment; the database drivers, the reactor work (if ever built) and the conformance migration are where estimates most often slip.

## 18. Open questions with recommended defaults

1. Folder and repository name: `zero-core` (default) or `zero-server-core`. Default: `zero-core`, because the pamoja precedent already separates folder from product name and the crates and packages all carry `zero-server`.
2. When `io-compio` becomes the default on Linux and Windows. Default: not before the section 5.7 gates are recorded on both backends, the 16-connection cause is identified and compio-driver is on a stable line covered by cargo-vet; if the gates show no CPU or memory advantage, `io-tokio` stays and the custom backend question closes.
3. Whether `tracing` is acceptable in the shipped graph under the `http3` feature. Default: yes, confined to the `http3` feature with its own deny.toml addendum and runtime-off, because an in-house QUIC transport is a multi-year audit commitment and quinn-proto is the only pure-Rust sans-I/O transport over rustls.
4. Brotli. Default: not in the shipped graph; ship gzip and DEFLATE in house in release 3 and revisit brotli as an opt-in feature with a named crate after a security review, since compression code is attack surface and the audit measured brotli q11 at 7.6 ms per 12 KB on dynamic bodies (carried).
5. mimalloc inside bindings. Default: never on by default; measure inside the three hosts on the harness and, if it wins there, offer it as an opt-in feature of the native package with the measured figures in the docs.
6. Python asyncio bridge: `call_soon_threadsafe` in house or pyo3-async-runtimes. Default: in house over `call_soon_threadsafe` with one post per batch; pyo3-async-runtimes only if the in-house bridge cannot complete coroutines without a per-request attach.
7. Free-threaded Python wheels. Default: abi3-py310 wheels for GIL builds in release 2, version-specific 3.13t and 3.14t wheels added when a free-threaded interpreter is in CI and the scaling has been measured.
8. WebTransport. Default: not implemented until the draft leaves Working Group Last Call; the `RawStreams` capability trait exists so that adding it never touches the h1 path.
9. Custom io_uring reactor. Default: deferred past release 3 and gated on an owner decision after the compio measurements; the specification in section 5.5 is kept so the work can start without new research.
10. HTTP/3 default-on. Default: runtime-off in release 3; promoted only after the interop runner, the CPU-per-request measurement and the NAT-rebinding tests pass.
11. The `zero-<capability>` names not probed here. Default: probe all of them in one session before the first publish and apply the `zero-server-<capability>` rule to any collision.
12. Overflow checks if they cost the Drogon comparison. Default: relax only for `zero-simd` through `[profile.release.package]`, never workspace-wide.
13. Certificate compression, `require_ems` strictness and session cache size. Default: off, on whenever TLS 1.2 is enabled (a deliberate departure from the rustls non-FIPS default of false, with the compatibility rationale in the option's documentation; section 6.7), 256.
15. Node inline-loop mode (the isolate thread hosting its Rust worker, no ThreadsafeFunction). Default: a release 2 experiment behind the harness row that runs the json test through a Node handler; it becomes the default only if it beats the isolate-per-core ThreadsafeFunction model on that row.
16. QUIC steering. Default: connection-id handoff over the seam's wake; the eBPF program is `http3.steering = "ebpf"` and reported by `zero doctor`.
17. Alt-Svc. Default: not emitted until the operator sets `http3.advertise` or `http3.probe_from`.
14. Which reference ceiling entry runs beside Drogon in the self-run. Default: libreactor (28,025,993 at zero errors, 39 microseconds at 16 connections in the research extraction), with faf as the second reference.

Measurements read from the earlier tasks: measure-tokio-tree.txt and measure-cargo-tree.txt (cargo 1.96.0).
